author: Kévin Drif
title: The North African family French critics couldn’t see
content:
Since her 2016 debut feature

Raw

, the French auteur Julia Ducournau’s films have been a staple of the body horror genre. Her movies reflect an unapologetic approach to exploring physical transformation and the “monstrous feminine,” an idea coined by feminist film scholar Barbara Creed to underscore the significance of gender and sexuality in the construction of monstrosity. In Ducournau’s films, female characters strive for emancipation from social and familial norms through cannibalism or transhumanism. Yet while

Raw

 and her sophomore feature

Titane

 (2021) center white protagonists,

Alpha

 (2025), her third film, foregrounds the complex dynamic of a family of North African descent, marking a significant departure for the auteur. Curiously, this demographic difference has been almost entirely absent from discussions of the film.

Set between the 1980s and 1990s,

Alpha

 follows its 13-year-old eponymous character; her mother, who is a doctor; and her uncle Amin as they confront a mysterious virus that transforms bodies into blue-veined marmoreal statues that eventually turn to dust. Critics have understandably focused on the epidemic narrative, the stigma attached to the infected, and its evocation of the AIDS crisis, but in doing so, they have overlooked another dimension of the story:

Alpha

 is one of the few contemporary French films to place a family of North African origin at the center of a national trauma.

Ducournau hardly conceals the central family’s roots. She casts actors of Algerian, Moroccan, and Iranian descent and the characters move between French and dialectal Arabic. In one scene that features the most cinematic French postcolonial locality — the

banlieue

 —

Alpha

 joins her extended family to share a couscous meal for an Eid celebration. The problem here is not simply that reviewers omitted demographic details but that their silence in effect reproduces a broader tendency and difficulty within French cultural discourse to see race, acknowledge colonial history, and address postcolonial belonging even when it permeates the screen.

Approaching

Alpha

 through a postcolonial lens opens more interpretative possibilities. Consider the body itself, a central concern of Ducournau’s cinema:

Alpha

’s makeshift tattoo, which symbolically binds her to Amin, evokes traditions of Amazigh inking while also drawing attention to the postcolonial body as a site of inscription, memory, and belonging. The gesture turns the body into a site where cultural memory can persist without being explicitly articulated;

Alpha

’s body becomes a postcolonial archive — a place where histories and affiliations that remain largely unspoken can nonetheless be inscribed, carried, and transmitted. Furthermore, the film’s concern with body regulation recalls the colonial politics of visibility explored by Frantz Fanon in his writings on French Algeria, where the control of bodies, especially female bodies through the practice of unveiling, functioned as a mechanism of domination.

Alpha

’s epidemic narrative also takes on new meanings when viewed through the history of North African migration. The AIDS crisis in France disproportionally affected marginalized communities. According to

a 1999 study

 led by the French Institut de veille sanitaire, or Institute of Health Surveillance, between 1978 and 1998, immigrant populations accounted for 14 percent of AIDS cases in France, when they only represented 6 percent of the adult population at the time. Drug users of North African origin infected through contaminated needles, much like Amin, represented the main mode of contamination for heterosexual men and accounted for 45 percent of North African immigrant cases. Still, they remain largely absent from narratives of the epidemic. This omission and silence of the infected is the result of the religious taboo attached to the disease and the larger structural disinterest in these populations. Ducournau’s attention to Amin gestures towards histories that have largely escaped commemoration.

Alpha

’s imagery of suffocation, disease, and social abandonment invites reflection of the lives and afterlives of colonial violence beyond France. The calcification of infected bodies recalls forms of historical petrification through which colonial atrocities are rendered distant, abstract, and invisible within French national memory. The structural and social segregation imposed on the sick in the film, illustrated in the …

author: Saif Eddine Ghobr
title: Capacity Substitution: How Tunisia’s Problems Became Someone Else’s Priorities
content:
In the summer of 2023, a young man from Gafsa tried to cross the Mediterranean on a small boat. He did not make it. His story is one of thousands — and it is increasingly understood by Tunisian institutions through the language of border management. It is also a story about who defines what a problem is.


In June 2023, the European Commission announced a package for Tunisia: up to

€900 million in proposed macro-financial assistance

,

€150 million in budget support

, and

€100 million for border management, search and rescue, anti-smuggling, and returns

. In July, the EU and Tunisia signed a

Memorandum of Understanding

 formalising the partnership. By September, a further

€105 million was allocated

 to migration-related programmes. By December, the €150 million budget-support programme was operational.


The sequence is documented. What it produces institutionally is less visible. This article examines a mechanism I call

capacity substitution

. Capacity building strengthens a state’s ability to solve its own problems. Capacity substitution makes a state more efficient at solving problems defined by someone else. The distinction is simple. Its consequences are not.


Consider Tunisia’s migration apparatus. The EU–Tunisia Memorandum links European support to border management, anti-smuggling operations, search and rescue, and returns. These are legitimate European objectives. They are also objectives that European institutions can define, fund, monitor, and measure. European support has equipped units, funded training, and strengthened interception capacity.


What it has not done — and was not designed to do — is strengthen Tunisia’s capacity to address the economic conditions that generate migration.

Youth unemployment stood at 35.4 percent in 2026

.

Graduate unemployment was 26.6 percent

. Regional inequality remains entrenched.


The argument is not that European funding caused these figures. It is that external funding concentrates institutional development on a specific set of functions. Those functions become better equipped, better staffed, and more internationally connected. The functions that would address the structural conditions producing migration are not developed through an equivalent institutional investment.  This is what capacity substitution describes.


A young unemployed person in Gafsa is unlikely to attempt to cross the Mediterranean simply because Tunisia lacks another surveillance system. The deeper driver is the narrowing of his economic and social horizon. If institutional capacity is concentrated on managing his departure, while the capacities that would address the conditions producing it are not developed through an equivalent investment, then the state becomes more effective at managing the symptom. It remains structurally less equipped to govern the cause. It does not require coercion. It does not require a conspiracy. It only requires that the external priority be better resourced than the domestic one.


Migration is not the only domain where this mechanism operates. European energy cooperation with Tunisia is another. EU funding for renewable energy, electricity interconnection, and green hydrogen is increasingly organised around projects that also serve European energy security: cross-Mediterranean interconnection such as the

ELMED project

, export capacity, and the

decarbonisation of European supply chains.


Domestic energy challenges  subsidy reform, grid reliability, and energy poverty are not absent from the relationship. But they are not the organising priority around which much of the external financing is structured. The result is a similar pattern: institutional capacity is strengthened in functions that serve externally defined priorities, while capacities addressing domestic structural conditions do not necessarily receive an equivalent institutional investment.


What migration and energy share is not a conspiracy. It is a logic. External resources tend to come attached to externally legible priorities. And externally legible priorities tend to be those that serve external needs.

Charles Moulthrope and USCGC Robert Goldman (WPC 1142) are en route to their new homeport in Bahrain in support of the Navy’s U.S. Fifth …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Beyond Translation: Reimagining Feminist Funding for Portuguese-Speaking Africa
content:
“Portuguese-speaking Africa is not on the margins of Africa’s feminist movement. It is an essential part of it.”


Across Africa, feminist movements have long challenged systems of inequality, responded to crises, created new possibilities for minoritized and excluded communities. Philanthropy has been integral to advances toward just and equal African societies. Yet within the current global and continental landscape of feminist philanthropy, some communities and movements remain largely unseen. 


The Portuguese-speaking African countries that include Angola, Cabo Verde, Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Equatorial Guinea and São Tomé and Principe, represent diverse histories, political realities and social contexts. Their feminist movements are dynamic, innovative and deeply rooted in their communities. They are advancing gender justice in contexts shaped by economic deprivation and inequality, climate change, difficult democratic transitions, shrinking civic space and gender-based violence.


Despite this important work, these movements continue to face significant barriers to accessing resources, networks and spaces where Africa’s feminist priorities are shaped. The challenge is not a lack of organizing. It is a fragmented funding ecosystem that has not yet fully recognized or responded to the diversity of Africa’s feminist movements. 


The cost of being overlooked


“This is not simply a language issue. It is a question of equity, power, and whose movements are seen as worthy of sustained investment.”


Language is often treated as a technical issue within philanthropy. But colonial imagined and erected linguistic borders, in reality, determine who participates, whose knowledge is shared, and which movements can access opportunities. Many continental funding opportunities, convenings, research publications and learning spaces are designed primarily in English or, to a lesser extent, French. Organizations from Portuguese-speaking countries frequently face additional costs related to translation, interpretation and participation — costs that are rarely built into funding models.


The result is a structural barrier: organizations with valuable expertise and strong community connections may remain disconnected from funding opportunities, regional conversations and shared learnings, not because of limited impact but because systems were not designed with their inclusion in mind. For philanthropy, this raises a fundamental question: 

What does meaningful inclusion look like when funding systems themselves create barriers to participation?


 


Listening before investing


At the African Women’s Development Fund (AWDF), we recognized that addressing this gap required more than acknowledging the challenge. It required listening, evidence and a deeper understanding of how feminist movements in Portuguese-speaking Africa organize, sustain themselves and envision their futures.


AWDF undertook a

mapping of feminist movements and funding landscapes

 across Portuguese-speaking Africa to better understand not only the barriers facing these movements, but also the opportunities for philanthropy to engage differently. We asked:

What does feminist organizing and funding actually look like across Portuguese-speaking Africa, and what would it take to strengthen these movements for the long term?


The findings provide an important reminder that communities and movements that have historically been overlooked are not waiting to be built. They are already organizing, innovating and creating solutions. What is needed is a funding ecosystem that recognizes their leadership and invests accordingly.


Feminist movements creating new pathways for change


Across the region, feminist organisations are demonstrating resilience, creativity, and strategic vision. There is growing interest in stronger Portuguese-speaking feminist networks that can support collective advocacy, shared learning, and cross-border solidarity. Storytelling and creative expression are being used as powerful organising tools, particularly among younger activists and in rural communities, allowing feminist narratives to emerge from local experiences and knowledge.  For example, our research shows that in São Tomé and Príncipe, informal associations are playing a vital role in mobilising communities through door-to-door outreach and storytelling, while in Equatorial Guinea, feminist collectives are using storytelling, dance, and performance as vehicles for feminist …

author: Awonusi Ayomide Jesudamilare
title: The Grid Inside the Grid
content:
In March, when

Cassava Technologies announced the launch of an AI factory powered by NVIDIA

 in South Africa, the company described it as a turning point. African businesses would gain local access to high-performance computing. Data would remain within African borders. Developers would be able to build models for local languages and local problems.


The promise matters. African researchers and firms cannot participate meaningfully in artificial intelligence if they must rent every unit of computing power from servers abroad. But the most consequential infrastructure inside an AI factory may not be the graphics processor. It may be the electricity connection.


Artificial intelligence is exceptionally energy hungry. The

International Energy Agency expects global electricity consumption by data centers to nearly double by 2030

. The pressure is not evenly distributed. Data centers cluster in particular cities and industrial corridors, where their demand can collide with already constrained transmission systems.


South Africa shows how this collision is being managed. Data center operators are increasingly securing electricity through private renewable plants and wheeling arrangements, which allow power generated in one province to travel across the national network to a customer elsewhere. Teraco, a major operator, is developing a 120-megawatt solar plant in the Free State to supply its facilities in Johannesburg and Cape Town.

Other operators have signed similar agreements

.


This can look like responsible investment. Private procurement adds renewable generation, reduces dependence on coal, and helps large customers avoid drawing all their electricity from local distribution networks.

South Africa’s electricity supply has also improved

 after years of blackouts. Yet the country still needs to

expand and strengthen its transmission network

. A private solar farm does not create a private route from the sun to a server. It still depends on substations, power lines, and grid capacity financed and governed as part of the national system.


The concern is not abstract. In May, community organizations

challenged plans for two Equinix data centers in Cape Town

, arguing that the applications did not provide enough information about electricity demand, water use, emissions, and backup power. The proposed facilities could require up to 160 megawatts combined. The dispute asks a basic democratic question: How should cities weigh private digital investment against competing claims on shared resources?


This is the grid inside the grid: a layer of firm, privately secured electricity built for facilities that cannot tolerate interruption, operating within a public system still struggling to expand transmission and connect new generation. The AI factory may be geographically located in South Africa, but its relationship to the surrounding economy can resemble an enclave. It receives dedicated power, imported equipment, sophisticated cooling, and backup generation. The wider public is promised future innovation, jobs, and growth.


The same tension is visible in Kenya. A proposed $1 billion data center involving Microsoft and the Emirati company G42 was presented as a geothermal-powered foundation for East Africa’s cloud and AI economy. By May 2026,

negotiations had stalled over requests for guaranteed capacity payments

, while the scale of the project’s power requirements remained under discussion. The episode revealed what investment announcements often conceal: Governments may be asked not only to host digital infrastructure but also to guarantee its market and reorganize scarce energy capacity around it.


None of this means African governments should reject data centers. Local computing capacity can reduce latency, support universities and startups, keep sensitive data closer to home, and create alternatives to total dependence on overseas cloud regions. The issue is not whether AI infrastructure should be built. It is whether public systems become stronger because it is built.


That requires more than celebratory language about sovereignty. Governments should disclose the electricity, water, land, tax, and guarantee arrangements attached to large data center projects. New power procurement should demonstrate that it adds generation rather than simply reserving existing transmission capacity. Contracts should require investment in shared grid infrastructure, meaningful local access to computing resources …

author: Abahlali_3
title: We Welcome the President’s Response to Femicide, but Much More Must Be Done
content:
1 October 2026 Abahlali baseMjondolo Women’s League Press Statement

We Welcome the President’s Response to Femicide, but Much More Must Be Done

On 28 September 2026, after 11 women had been murdered in Ekurhuleni since July, Abahlali baseMjondolo and other residents of Ekurhuleni marched in Kempton Park against the killing of women and the failure of the police to adequately protect women from violence. We handed a memorandum to the Kempton Park Police Station and Ekurhuleni District Management.

•⁠ ⁠A public report on the investigations into the 11 murders, presented at an open public meeting. •⁠ ⁠A well-funded and properly equipped women-led GBV task team for the townships and shack settlements of Ekurhuleni. •⁠ ⁠A 24-hour Victim Support Room at Kempton Park Police Station with properly trained female officers. •⁠ ⁠Daily visible and women-friendly policing in high-risk areas, with additional patrols at night and on weekends. •⁠ ⁠A public audit of all GBV cases reported in Ekurhuleni since July. •⁠ ⁠An open public meeting at which the police must account to the women of Ekurhuleni for failures in responding to GBV and femicide. •⁠ ⁠The election of a women’s committee to which the police must report every week on their work relating to GBV and femicide.

We therefore welcome much of what President Cyril Ramaphosa announced in his address to the nation on 29 September.

The investigation into the Ekurhuleni killings has been elevated to the national level, a specialised multidisciplinary investigation is under way and visible policing in Ekurhuleni has been increased.

The President also announced a national case-recovery operation for unresolved murders, attempted murders, rapes and serious sexual offences involving women and children. The commitment to audit unresolved cases, identify delays and establish recovery plans for stalled cases is in accordance with the demands that we made in Kempton Park.

He made a commitment to address forensic backlogs, give urgent priority to forensic evidence in cases involving the rape and murder of women and children, and report publicly on progress.

The President has also made it clear that women must not be turned away by the police, that protection orders must be enforced, that dockets must not disappear and that women reporting violence must be treated with dignity. These are all issues raised directly in our memorandum.

Along with all these measures we strongly welcome the announcement that every municipality must conduct a women’s safety audit. Broken streetlights, unsafe transport routes, abandoned buildings and neglected public spaces all place women in danger. In shack settlements a lack of lighting, unsafe or absent toilets and unsafe routes through our communities put women and girls at risk every day. We need safe and reliable public transport, including at night and early in the morning, and safe routes between our homes, transport stops, workplaces, schools and shops.

We strongly support the President’s recognition that harmful alcohol use is ‘a significant aggravating factor in interpersonal violence’, his call for the stronger enforcement of liquor laws and his instruction that a package of laws and enforcement measures to reduce alcohol-related violence be put before Cabinet within 60 days. This must include reducing the excessive concentration of alcohol outlets, restricting trading hours and enforcing clear closing times, tighter licensing controls, and much stronger regulation of alcohol advertising, promotion and sponsorship. Government must regulate the alcohol industry and resist corporate pressure to weaken, delay or block effective regulation. The long-delayed Liquor Amendment Bill should be revived and debated urgently. Serious regulation of the alcohol industry is a critical part of the struggle against violence in general.

But much more needs to be done.

Women cannot just be called to meetings to be informed about decisions that have already been taken for us without us. Women must have real power and working class and poor women, who are the majority, must have real power.

This is why our memorandum demanded an elected women’s committee to which each police station must report every week. Democratically organised women must be able to demand information about investigations, police response times, missing dockets, failures to enforce protection orders and complaints against police.

Every woman must also have the right to know who is …

author: Caleb Okereke
title: Matthew Blaise wants to be your friend and neighbor
content:
Matthew Blaise and I must have been in our mid teens when we first met. I don’t remember the exact year, but I remember that it was on Facebook. It did not take long for that online connection to become a real friendship, and it is one that has persisted despite life carrying us in different directions.   


When we sit down for this conversation in September, I am in Philadelphia and Matthew is in Brazil. He is preparing for

Friends and Neighbors

, a new art and literary festival in Lagos built around a deceptively simple question: What responsibility do we have to the people we call our friends and our neighbors?


It is a question that makes our own friendship an interesting place from which to begin. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 


Caleb:

 Something I find provocative about the title “Friends and Neighbors” is that you also seem to be making a statement about the ways queerness shows up in the ordinary. I’m thinking about this song, “Your driver could be LGBT, your friend could be LGBT, your neighbour could be LGBT.” Was that part of the conceptual framing?


Matthew:

 Actually, that’s another way to see it. When I thought of this concept, I thought of proximity within our community. A trip from Lagos to Europe is cheaper than a trip from Lagos to Abidjan, which is a neighboring country. For me, that’s a metaphor for what a lot of friendship within the African continent, especially around queerness, has been due to bad policy, homophobia and criminalization.


Queer people within Africa are not so familiar with themselves. And in that sense, we really haven’t constructed what queer Africanness is because we are still not so close to ourselves. But I find it interesting that you also see it from the point of everyday life, where people you come in contact with could be of this community or could possess these identities without you knowing.


Caleb:

 That’s what immediately came to my attention. Even when you say, “Hello, friends. Hello, neighbors,” you’re talking to all of us, right? It’s not “queer friends and neighbors.” The implicit read is that even if you’re straight, queer people are all around you. They’re your friends. They’re your neighbors. They might not tell you that they’re queer, but they’re there.


Matthew:

 From the perspective of bell hooks, societies should be built on love and friendship. This very important foundation of love has been taken away from queer people, or we’ve not been given that due to our queerness. Governmental policies and criminalization also make us live our lives in isolation. What it means to be friends right now is also very transactional, especially for queer people.


Caleb:

 One thing that has defined our friendship, at least for me, is honesty. There are things I can tell you that I can’t tell anybody else, obviously, so a sort of radical honesty. And as you were talking about transactional relationships, it made me think, what is the place of honesty in friendship, especially in a context where being honest about yourself can carry consequences?


Matthew:

 I think you don’t owe everyone that truth about yourself. For those who I truly trust, I owe them that responsibility of truth. And I do believe, for every friendship, there has to be that investment in honesty.


Caleb:

 But friendship in and of itself is a risk. I don’t think we realize that, but every friendship is a risk.


Matthew:

 Yeah, friendship sometimes, I mean, it’s not a constant state of feeling a certain way. It’s a roller coaster of emotions. It’s a journey. It’s an adventure. So you encounter a lot of things on the way.


You stretch your hand to someone and they actually bite your hand, then you know they are not really having that good intention towards you. So you can decide to stretch your hand again or push them away. But for me, I think it’s important that we’re able to stretch our hands and bring people together and do the work of educating them until we just know they’re irredeemable.


Caleb:

 Yeah…


Matthew:

 What responsibility do you think you owe me as your friend?


Caleb:

 You are now the one asking me questions. But no, I mean, I think you owe your friend loyalty. That’s one of the things that I’m non-negotiable on. I mean, there are many other things you owe your friend.


Matthew:

 You owe them honesty also?


Caleb:

 You owe them honesty. You also owe your friends grace. I give grace a lot. Maybe it’s not even grace. I’m also like, oh …

author: WoMin
title: Women on the frontlines: Organise, Educate, Liberate, Celebrate!
content:
Across social justice movements, both in the Present and in the Past, education has been a central piece binding theory and praxis. It is from this understanding that, from the 17

th

 to the 18

th

 of September, the

Afro-International Feminist Organising School (AFRO-IFOS),

 a movement building space that uses popular education to strengthen our collective knowledge, share our experiences, and grow our international movement, hosted a School of Facilitators in Nairobi, Kenya, to support the deepening of a Decolonial Feminist Popular Education praxis across the more than 30 countries and territories represented, from Africa and the Americas.


There is power in naming the inequalities and wounds we carry as peoples who have been dispossessed of land, livelihoods, cultures and Knowledge. However, our greatest challenge is creating spaces that encourage us to dream of a world beyond the limits of colonial imagination.


Popular education has been a powerful practice for creating such spaces. Rooted in the knowledge and lived experiences of the people, it invites us to learn not only from books and institutions, but from one another.


Education is a political commitment


In the 1971 BBC film “

Behind the lines

”, Maria, a Mozambican guerrilla fighter explains that education was at the heart of why she decided to join the liberation struggle. In her experience

“If a girl reached a certain class [The colonialists] said that is enough for us, Africans.”


(Literacy Campaign, Guerrilla warfare in Angola, 1968. Photo: Augusta Conchiglia)


Our feminist

herstories

 across Africa and beyond have been deeply shaped by anti-colonial struggles. It was within the liberation movements that many women and men encountered education as a practice of freedom, in learning to question colonial power, reclaiming their histories and wisdom, fighting to protect their sovereignty and imagining forms of collective life beyond the impositions of heteropatriarchal, capitalist, colonial systems.


As feminist ancestor Nawal El Saadawi reminds us

“good education means creating dissatisfaction and disobedience.”

 Her wordsspeak to the transformative power of education to nurture the critical consciousness needed to both understand the conditions that constrain us and to connect them to our personal experiences, which is fundamental to organise collectively towards liberation.


But liberation cannot be achieved by a few, full liberation requires all of us. Our political project must be sustained by an intentional educational project that deepens our proposals and equips us to build the worlds we envision.


The educator is a pollinator


Through processes of learning, unlearning, relearning and imagining together, we become both teachers and students in our movements. This is one of the many ways in which decolonial feminist popular education inspires us to cultivate relational ways of working together that are grounded in mutual learning, listening, solidarity and care.


Instead of positioning the educator as the one who holds all the answers, popular educators create spaces where all can collectively formulate the questions that emerge from our struggles and where all can develop the knowledge needed to respond.


“Vou aprender a ler

 /

Para ensinar minhas camaradas

 /

I will learn how to read

 /

To teach my comrades”


Brazilian struggle song


The same way bees are essential for healthy environments, popular educators are an important part of feminist movements infrastructure. Popular educators nurture the power that already exists within movements.


Like the flower, each individual carries something that can nourish the collective. Learning is never only for ourselves. What we learn becomes a good we carry around our movements, to share, to exchange, to teach and to transform. Knowledge moves between us, allowing new ideas, possibilities and material actions to be activated. It is through this circulation of knowledge that we can produce the sweet taste of hope needed to build different futures.


Organising and liberating as we educate


“The beast is too big, and we need a political project that inspires us to build something every day and not just to fight and destroy the world as we know it.” –


Sandra, Guatemala


A decolonial feminist popular education praxis can build bridges across our different struggles, experiences, beliefs and movements, creating the conditions to move beyond simply resisting what exists …

author: Hassan Alnaser, Mohamed Alagra, Mashair Idris
title: Ethiopia accuses Sudan of backing opposition, reshuffled hope for Idris’s govt, tribal violence engulfs South Darfur, military opens road to West Kordofan, China on Sudan’s coast
content:
Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter


here

.


Sudan’s government is taking a long hard look in the mirror, and they don’t like what they see, sources close to Prime Minister Kamel Idris and the Transitional Sovereignty Council

told

 Mada Masr this week.

 


Ushered in on a promise of hope a year ago, Idris’s government has faced significant issues. Some of those come down to war-time trials, but infighting and attempts to delimit the remit of a civilian government backed by a powerful and intrusive military council have been persistent issues. 


Now the government is considering a reshuffle of ministerial and gubernatorial appointments to address executive imbalances and shortfalls, particularly on economic and service-related issues, according to a source in Idris’s office.


While Idris and the TSC may see an administrative reshuffle as a way to address war-time woes, the armed movements that signed the 2020 Juba peace agreement insist that any bureaucratic rearrangement must not change the power-sharing agreement inked in the South Sudanese capital. 


For now, the reshuffle is all just talk. But the movements do not view it in isolation from the larger reshaping of the political landscape of recent months, a leader in one of the Juba armed movements told Mada Masr, particularly as the planned national dialogue will have to address their relationship with the government.


Outside military-controlled areas, the Rapid Support Forces have also been dealing with internal discord over the last two weeks, though the dispute they are presiding over has a decidedly less understanding and diplomatic tenor. 


Throughout September, deadly inter-tribal clashes have engulfed South Darfur. With heavy weapons in hand and grappling with a faltering rainy season, tribes in Gereida, about 90 km south of Nyala, and in southern parts of Nyala itself, have become embroiled in violent confrontations. 


The RSF has tried to step in to calm the situation, deploying troops to prevent it from continuing to spiral out of control. As residents look on to see how effective these immediate tamping down measures will be, civil society and RSF sources agree that the much more difficult problem will be halting the spread of heavy weapons into residential communities, which allows competition over water, pasture and farmland during droughts to become increasingly militarized. 


On Sudan’s battlefields this week, the military cleared the last major RSF defensive positions in North Kordofan, effectively opening the West Kordofan front. These losses have triggered yet another defection from the paramilitary group, as Al-Tayeb “Waheedo” Mohamed Ahmed arrived to Omdurman, saying he left after witnessing “tragedies” and “collapse” within the RSF’s ranks.


But while frontline battles remain consequential, drone warfare continues to figure in Sudan’s conflict. RSF drones struck targets in Gezira and North Kordofan over the week, reaching fuel infrastructure east of Wad Madani and multiple sites in Obeid, where at least six civilians were killed.


This week also saw a series of tense diplomatic exchanges. The first came at the UN General Assembly’s  debate on Monday, with the United Arab Emirates and Sudanese delegations engaging in tug-of-war over the narrative on Sudan’s conflict. A former official said the spat does not necessarily signal another diplomatic rupture. 


But the second tense diplomatic moment could prove more consequential. Ethiopia, recently plunged into another civil war, accused Sudan of abetting opposition fighters then took the more drastic diplomatic step of expelling Eritrean and Egyptian diplomats. 


While wars and their fallout dominate the headlines this week, Sudan is taking steps toward a post-war future. And as with previous attempts to attract foreign powers to Khartoum, this future projection involves lucrative real estate on Sudan’s Red Sea coast. 


But instead of Russia or the UAE, this time, it is China that is coming in to revive the Abu Amama port project, two years after Sudan cancelled a memorandum of understanding with an Emirati-led consortium to execute the project.

author: Ndivhuwo Mukwevho
title: Limpopo district hospital ‘filthy’, ‘broken’ and leaderless
content:
Filthy conditions, a shortage of warm water, a broken emergency communications system, and unresolved complaints from nurses are some of the adversities being faced by both patients and healthcare workers at Nkhensani hospital in Giyani, Limpopo.


The root cause


According to healthcare workers stationed at the hospital, the woes at the public facility are fuelled by a lack of leadership. For the past eight years, the hospital has not had a permanent CEO. Five individuals have, in ten years, acted as CEOs on a temporary basis but were never permanently appointed.


The Limpopo department of health has blamed a lack of suitable candidates as the main reason for not appointing a permanent CEO. The CEO position has been vacant since 2016 following the removal of Themba Mhlanga.


“We are leaderless at this hospital and everyone does what they want; hence everything is a mess at Nkhensani. I can confidently tell that at night, patients at this hospital bath using cold water as warm water gets finished in the early hours of the morning; and the kitchen does not operate during the night and those who want tea or coffee are always left wanting,” said a staff nurse stationed at Nkhensani hospital.


Lives of patients at risk


The nurse further said that the hospital is filthy and rarely cleaned: “This hospital is never cleaned, we often go for days without it being cleaned and no one cares and cleaners are also never reprimanded as there is no one to reprimand them and they do as they like. This puts the lives of patients and healthcare workers at risk.”


The emergency communications system has not been working for months at the hospital and nurses are forced to use their personal cell phones during emergencies. “Alerting doctors of emergencies at this hospital has become extra difficult as we have to use our own personal cell phones because the hospital does not have a working emergency dial; it has not been working for months. What if I do not have airtime and a patient is in need of a doctor urgently? It might lead to an avoidable death of a patient,” she said.


The nurse also told

Elitsha

 that she has personally raised most of these issues with previous acting CEOs but nothing has ever been done to address her concerns. “Even if you complain to those superior to you, nothing is ever done to address your concerns. No one is prepared to take responsibility and all this has got to do with the lack of leadership at Nkhensani hospital,” she said.


Derrick Mashaba, a local community member in Giyani residing about 2 kilometres away from Nkhensani, told

Elitsha

 that he has witnessed the tumble of the hospital over the past decade. “We have witnessed the fall of our precious hospital over the past ten years. We have seen overcrowding, dilapidating buildings, shortage of water and lack of leadership, and all this has contributed to the fall of the mighty hospital,” said Mashaba.


It hurts him to see the fall of the hospital which is so close to his home. “This is a district hospital and it is supposed to be the best in our region but it is not being prioritised. A hospital as big as this one cannot operate without a permanent CEO; it is wrong and it is something which is supposed to be addressed immediately,” he said.


Limpopo health spokesperson, Neil Shikwambana said that the department is working towards appointing a permanent CEO. “The recruitment process is underway and an acting CEO has been appointed to ensure continuity during this process,” he said.

author: Feven Merid
title: Where the mouse eats the cat
content:
“Welcome to the Central Prison of Douala,” La PJ, an inmate and a star of the documentary

Jail Time Records

, says in an opening scene of the film. “The place where the mouse eats the cat.” Dione Roach, one of the film’s directors, offered me an interpretation: “The world is upside down in prison; the mouse can be more shrewd,” she said. The intimate glimpse into the Central Prison of Douala, also known as New Bell Prison, does indeed reveal an upside-down world. Like many prisons, its inmates recreate the contours of outside life on the inside, but in New Bell it’s taken to another level. There are actual neighborhoods like the Latin Quarter, home to the Emperor and his gang known as the Latinos, and the Base, where the prisoners who make up the quasi police squad reside. There’s a marketplace for people to sell fried foods and taxis, except these taxis are inmates who swiftly run through the congested prison to hand-deliver messages. They even have a “homeless” population, those who must sleep outside in the courtyard because there aren’t enough beds. Their neighborhood is dubbed House of the Penguins.

This all comes into focus when you learn New Bell is notoriously overcrowded — it was built for 800 people but currently holds almost 6,000. Thus, the prison has been transformed into a mini city, colloquially referred to by inmates as the 11th province of Cameroon (there are officially 10). La PJ, a lanky and charismatic man dressed in his uniform of a conductor’s hat, blazer, and tie, steps in as mayor to give us the lay of the land. “Our jewel of jewels,” he says, as he approaches his final stop on this tour — a recording studio. Specifically, it’s the Jail Time Records studio, for which the film is named and the reason for its making.

Jail Time Records, the recording studio, is the first to be put in an African prison, according to the film’s directors and the studio’s founders Dione Roach and Steve Happi. The two run it as a nonprofit music label for inmates and those who are readjusting to life outside of prison. From its start in 2018, the duo has been documenting the studio’s impact; first, inadvertently, through shooting music videos and then with the intention to make a documentary. Roach, who is from Italy and has been based in Cameroon since 2017, has served as the studio’s artistic director, and Happi, who is from Cameroon, as its lead producer (Happi was incarcerated at New Bell for two years, during which time he met Roach and helped get the studio up and running). Shot over six years, they’ve created a film that captures the curiosities of New Bell remarkably well (

Jail Time Records

 won top prizes at Tribeca Film Festival in New York). A few weeks ago, I spoke to the two directors over Zoom about what it’s like documenting New Bell, the music of their main characters, and how the film let them show a fuller picture of life in prison. This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Feven Merid

How did you start Jail Time Records and when did you realize you wanted to make a film about it?

Dione Roach

I was volunteering, doing art courses, and I came across a group of really talented musicians. They were incarcerated, and I just had the idea to do an album with them. And then I was even like, why just an album? Why don’t we actually build something that can stay and be used by many people? And so I proposed the recording studio to the prison, and they accepted, and we got it built. And then that’s when I met Steve, who was incarcerated at the time, and he was already a music producer and sound engineer. Someone introduced us, and I was finished volunteering, so I left him the keys of the studio. I came back a few months after, and they’d been doing like so much work and recording, and it had really become this like place of like extreme creativity and outlet.

Steve Happi

Before even starting the movie, I was already doing music videos and having access with the camera inside prison when I was still incarcerated. So as she said, it was just a natural process, and having access with the camera and such intimate moments of our life and our journey, we started recording everything.

Feven Merid

What was it like to film inside such a crowded place?

Dione Roach

At the start, we went with a friend who had like a gigantic camera, and he didn’t already work in prison as well, like so they didn’t know him, and so it just wasn’t really the right setup, you know, for that kind of space and …

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Nunavut sports hall of fame inductions begin
content:
The Nunavut Sport Federation will induct its hall of fame’s inaugural class this weekend at the Aqsarniit hotel in Iqaluit.


The ceremony will take place during the Sport and Recreation Awards gala, where the Government of Nunavut recognizes the territory’s athletes, administrators, volunteers and coaches, according to a news release issued Friday by the Recreation and Parks Association of Nunavut.


Former NHL player Jordin Tootoo and Inuit games athlete Attima Hadlari are the first inductees into the hall.


Doors open to the gala at 6:30 p.m. The ceremony begins at 7 p.m.


From 2003 to 2017, Tootoo, played 723 games for the Nashville Predators, Detroit Red Wings, New Jersey Devils and Chicago Blackhawks. He racked up 65 goals, 96 assists and 1,010 penalty minutes during that time.


Hadlari was an Arctic sports athlete from Cambridge Bay who mastered the sealskin whip and went on to coach and officiate for young athletes participating in traditional Inuit games.


He also served in the first Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit Katimajiit, which gives expertise in how to apply Inuit traditional knowledge in government, from 2003 to 2005.


Each year, the Nunavut Sports and Recreation Hall of Fame plans to take nominations from community members for inductees.

title: In photos: Nations mark Orange Shirt Day in Manitoba, Saskatchewan
content:
Daniella Peltier with an Every Child Matters flag at the Southern Chiefs’ Organization’s Orange Shirt Day powwow at the Canada Life Centre in Winnipeg on September 30. Photo by Crystal Greene


Indigenous communities across “Canada” marked the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation — also known as Orange Shirt Day — with various gatherings and events on Sept. 30.


On the prairies, IndigiNews reporters Crystal Greene and Brittany Boschman attended gatherings in or near their own communities. Both reporters photographed the day’s events, capturing the spirit of each and honouring their own connections to the story.


In Winnipeg, Crystal attended a commemorative walk and powwow that was hosted by the Southern Chiefs’ Organization at Canada Life Centre.


In Saskatchewan in the Qu’Appelle Valley, Brittany was present for a community gathering and walk hosted by the Star Blanket Cree Nation. You can find a selection of their photos below.


Women who survived residential “schools” took part in a powwow dance special, honouring survivors in Winnipeg on Orange Shirt Day. Photos by Crystal Greene


Male survivors of residential “schools” were also honoured during a dance special at the Winnipeg Orange Shirt Day powwow. Photo by Crystal Greene


There was a sea of orange, interspersed with powwow dancers, during the intertribal dances of the Orange Shirt Day powwow in Winnipeg. Photo by Crystal Greene


In Lebret, SK, two people stand outside the White Calf Gymnasium, waiting for the walk to begin. The mural was painted by Darren Pratt in 2022. Photo by Brittany Boschman


In Lebret, SK, an eagle with outstretched wings hovers above while people walk. Created by Darren Pratt, the mural on the White Calf Gymnasium depicts an eagle stretching across the building, with figures holding hands beneath it and tipis surrounding the landscape. Photo by Brittany Boschman


People wearing orange shirts walk through the Wa-Pii Moos-Toosis White Calf Gymnasium, one of the last remaining structures of the former Lebret Indian Residential School. Photo by Brittany Boschman


Three young participants walk along the path toward the former gate of the residential school. The Smudge Walk began at the gymnasium, continued through the community and returned to the former school grounds. Photo by Brittany Boschman

author: Arezu Fayyazi
title: Afghan Women Are Restricted, But They Cannot Be Silenced. They Continue to Be Agents of Change in Afghanistan.
content:
Afghan women have been living under one of the most repressive systems in the world, as the Taliban continue to impose restrictive edicts – over 160 in total to date. These orders restrict their ability to work, attend school, move freely and even leave their homes without a male guardian. Yet despite the barriers the Taliban have imposed, Afghan women continue to be at the forefront of efforts to build peace and stability in Afghanistan.

Peace and security extends beyond just political conversations. They also include the “daily strategies Afghan women employ to defend human rights and generate conditions for peace.” According to a report by the Georgetown Institute for Women, Peace, and Security, 81% of Afghan women participate in efforts focused on women’s and girl’s education, 64% in economic empowerment, and another 54% in health & reproductive rights and services. Afghan women are also engaged in health and reproductive rights and services, by roughly 9%, compared to women from other regions of South Asia.

These figures demonstrate the perseverance, leadership, and problem solving of Afghan women. Afghanistan is facing a reproductive health crisis, with maternal mortality rapidly increasing since the Taliban took over in 2021. The loss of international funding and organizational support has also greatly affected the reproductive health programs. To help fill these gaps and address the mounting health issues facing women and girls, Afghan women have stepped in to provide critical support and services.

This sense of responsibility extends beyond just responding to immediate needs; it reflects the determination of Afghan women to protect and strengthen their communities despite the restrictions imposed on them. While many formal opportunities for education, employment, and political participation have been taken away after 2021, women have continued to find ways to serve their communities. For example, they have established online schools, supported women’s access to healthcare services, organized community-based initiatives, and advocated for women’s rights.

The significant role women continue to play in activities that promote peace and security demonstrate that resilience is not just their ability to endure oppression. It is also the ability to adapt, organize, and create solutions especially in an environment that has been designed to limit their every move and every opportunity.

Their resilience is particularly significant because many of these efforts occur in an environment where women are already facing risks to their lives. Their actions demonstrate their collective responsibility, where women have repeatedly stepped forward to address unmet needs themselves.

Their resilience also challenges the perception of Afghan women in the media solely as victims of the Taliban restrictions imposed on them. While challenges of these restrictions are severe, Afghan women have found ways to find space and operate within them. They are evidence that resilience can take many forms.

Their efforts demonstrate that, even under deeply restrictive circumstances, Afghan women continue to shape the social fabric of their communities and contribute to building a more stable and peaceful Afghanistan. This is also evident in how Afghan women see and define themselves. Among women working in the peace and security field, 65% of women describe themselves as activists while 37% of them describe themselves as human rights defenders. As one activist explained, “As an activist woman, I am not a victim of war, but an architect of social peace, and this is a voice that must be heard globally.”

Their work in education, healthcare, economic empowerment, and community development demonstrates that Afghan women are not simply recipients of aid or victims of conflict, they are powerful agents of change. Their persistence and leadership are an important source of strength for their communities and a reminder that peacebuilding in Afghanistan cannot succeed without the full participation of Afghan women at the table.

author: Elizabeth Weill-Greenberg
title: Activists Are Pushing Cities and Companies to Cancel Parking Contracts With ICE
content:
The Trump administration’s abduction and deportation machine is multifaceted. There are clear-cut components — agents, shackles, and jails — and less obvious, although no less essential, ones — cars and parking spaces.


In an effort to impede the attacks on immigrants, mayors of some of the country’s largest cities, including

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani

,

Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson

, and

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu

, have issued executive orders

banning Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)

 from using city-owned parking lots and properties.


But even in cities where mayors have banned ICE from using government-owned properties, ICE still has free reign to contract with private companies. After the federal agency

posted a notice

 seeking “Surge Parking” in 14 cities, including Boston, Wu

released a public letter

 to

local parking garage and lot owners

, warning them that if ICE were “to procure such resources, it would constitute an unprovoked and unwarranted escalation, creating potentially significant risks to public safety and halting economic activity across our entire region.”


“Today, I ask you to join us: Reject any proposition by ICE to facilitate an attack on the people of Boston,”

she wrote

. “In the face of escalating attacks on cities across the country, we have repeatedly seen that the strongest defense is solidarity.”


In the Boston suburb of Burlington, Massachusetts, Bearing Witness New England has been holding weekly protests outside ICE’s Boston Field Office, where people are

held for days

 in inhumane conditions. Activists say ICE has been keeping its vehicles in a nearby parking lot owned by local developer National Development.


According to a report by

NPR

 affiliate

WBUR

, the company sent a letter to local activists in February, stating that ICE vehicles were being “improperly parked” in its parking spaces, and that it had “reached an arrangement with ICE that they would no longer park their vehicles on our property.”


However, the company also said that the government agency, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), has

rights to use the garage

 and the company does not have authority over how the FAA parcels out parking spaces to other federal agencies, according to

WBUR

’s report.


Nathan Phillips, a Boston University professor who organizes with the Burlington-area coalition

Building Up Resilience Networks (B.U.R.N.)

, says ICE has continued to park in sections of lots National Development leases to the FAA that exceed what the lease allows.


Protests that target parking garages are “throwing sand in the gears” of ICE’s deportation and abduction machine, he says.


“So much of their operation depends on logistics of transport and travel,” Phillips told

Truthout

. “It’s human trafficking, and so if we can go after the trafficking, the means by which they’re doing this, that can have a really effective impact.”


The Appeal in Your Inbox


Subscribe to our newsletters for regular updates, analysis and context straight to your email.


          Sign Up


Fellow B.U.R.N. activist Josh Model says National Development’s recent actions contradict its public image as a

philanthropic company

 committed to improving communities.


“National Development Corporation, which, as a local developer, likes to promote that they’re cognizant of community needs and give to charity and all these nice things,” but they’re “letting ICE stage kidnappings” from their property, said Model.


While the government spending website,

usaspending.gov

, only lists 12 active contracts for parking spaces, as of September 28, the true number of parking lots that ICE uses is likely much higher, said Model. It’s difficult to untangle where ICE is parking, in part, because many of the contracts are not with ICE, but through another federal agency, the

General Services Administration

 (GSA), he said. The GSA manages government buildings and real estate, and owns or leases space in more than 8,300 buildings, according to an

explainer

 on the agency published by the Congressional Research Service.


In the case of National Development, ICE is using parking leased by the GSA for the FAA, according to Model.

PPA website

 states that, among other responsibilities, it coordinates “the efforts of public agencies concerning parking” and establishes and operates public …

author: Valerie Anne
title: Lili Reinhart Wants To Adapt a Lesbian Vampire Novella — Let Her!
content:
feature image photo by Emma McIntyre / Staff via Getty Images

Bisexual baddie Lili Reinhart has been on a press tour for her new film, The Love Hypothesis, and I’ve been really enjoying her interviews. The film seems to be the CLASSIC fake dating trope come to life — in fact, the book it’s based on started as Star Wars fanfic! — and despite the movie being seemingly extremely heterosexual, on this tour, she has been quick to remind interviewers and fans that she’s queer. She has also said she hopes in her next project is gay. (Fingers crossed!)

In one video interview she says, “I’m instantly way more interested in doing a movie if my character is a little gay,” she continued. “Because I’m a little gay.” She also reads a comment about being one of “the five pillars of bisexuality with preference to women” and she called it an honor.

In that same interview, she also mentioned that she’s trying to get a film adaptation of a lesbian vampire novella made but that Hollywood seems “too afraid” to make it. She also wonders aloud who WOULDN’T want to make it, a sentiment I agree with. The general assumption people have been making is that it would be an adaptation of the 1872 novella Carmilla, which the popular webseries starring Natasha Negovanlis and Elise Bauman was based on, and I think that would be fun if true. I personally think there can’t be too many adaptations of that novella. The gayer the better. In fact, I just read Hungerstone by Kat Dunn, which is one of a few retellings of that novella and offers a very different take than the webseries.

I, for one, am delighted that Lili keeps making her press tour about a heterosexual love story as queer as she can, and I’m glad she’s using it to pitch her idea. I really hope someone with the means is paying attention and can pick it up and let her run with it.

In my opinion, there’s no such thing as too many lesbian vampire adaptations in general. When is someone going to make a Bury Our Bones in the Midnight Soil miniseries? A movie version of A Long Time Dead, anyone? Let’s get all the lesbian vampires out here while we’re at it. Tis the season!

title: Ruthanna Emyrs, A Half-Built Garden, Tor 2022
content:
Recensione a cura di

Kevin Carson

. Originale:

A Half-Built Garden, by Ruthanna Emrys (Tor 2022)

, del 29 luglio 2026. Traduzione italiana di

Enrico Sanna

.


A Half-Built Garden

 è una storia di contatto alieno ben congegnata, dalla trama avvincente, cose che da sole fanno una piacevole lettura. Come forse saprà chi ha già letto altre mie recensioni, quando recensisco storie di fantascienza ambientate in un futuro prossimo utopico, libero e postcapitalista, il mio interesse riguarda anche come questo mondo è strutturato. Un peccatuccio che condivido con Auden che scrive ispirandosi alla bibbia.


Siamo negli anni 2080, dopo l’Età delle Turbolenze di metà secolo, e il mondo emerge dalle rovine del capitalismo per creare una nuova, tollerabile società.


La principale istituzione di governo è la watershed network, una federazione di istituzioni locali autogestite grossomodo corrispondenti alle bioregioni, comprendente gran parte della popolazione e delle risorse mondiali. L’equilibrio di potere è il risultato di una rivoluzione perlopiù nonviolenta iniziata una o due generazioni prima e finita verso il 2050: una serie di boicottaggi, sabotaggi e altre azioni dirette spingono le aziende economiche a rinchiudersi in enclave in alto mare. La vicenda è narrata attraverso gli occhi di un abitante della Chesapeake Watershed, che ricorda quando i suoi genitori “mettevano i primi sensori vietati nel fiume Potomac e barricavano le fabbriche per imporre la volontà collettiva della nascente rivoluzione dandelion.”


Le aziende sono perlopiù “padroni miliardari e dipendenti servi ammassati dietro il filo spinato nelle loro isole artificiali.” Tranne “qualche convertito e visitatore”, gli abitanti sono “i discendenti delle persone arrivate con il loro fondatore: dipendenti e sodali che preferivano scappare dall’apocalisse piuttosto che unirsi in comunità e evitarla.”


Le enclave aziendali sono circondate da “filo spinato” evidentemente imposto dalle watershed durante la rivoluzione. “Finalmente abbiamo vietato le aziende. Mio padre e altri, che hanno dato vita alla prima rete del cambiamento, hanno operato per fermarle.” La rivoluzione “limita la produzione di CO

2

 per contenere il riscaldamento climatico bloccando i trasporti quando si supera il limite.” Le aziende, “refrattarie al cambiamento, … finiscono per barricarsi dietro il filo spinato in alcune isole artificiali…”


Esiliate nelle isole, gran parte delle aziende, che “già da tempo hanno perso ogni parvenza di legalità”, rifiuta qualunque riconoscimento ufficiale dalle watershed. Inviano osservatori ai dialoghi sulla CO

2

, obbediscono tacitamente alle limitazioni dell’anidride e di altri inquinanti che le watershed, attori principali, impongono loro, e imbrogliano pensando di poter sfuggire ai controlli. Data la loro relativa debolezza, sono costrette a chiedere il permesso delle watershed consorziate quando l’impatto delle loro attività supera i confini.


Gran parte delle funzioni economiche delle società, tolte alcune zone che hanno ancora il monopolio del know-how, sono state rilevate dalle watershed. Comprese certe istituzioni industriali risalenti al periodo precedente, come il “MIT e l’Associazione di costruttori panasiatica” che sono “collegati alle reti dandelion”.


Le relazioni tra watershed e aziende sono generalmente da guerra fredda.


“Compriamo ancora da loro, saltuariamente… Cose che ci servono e che ancora non siamo riusciti a riprodurre con l’ingegneria a ritroso, oppure pratichiamo qualche scambio nella speranza di indurli a unirsi a noi. Quando succede, lasciamo che visitino le watershed, purché promettano di comportarsi bene.”


Nel loro rapporto con le aziende, il compito principale delle watershed è la gestione del declino: cercano di rilevarne le funzioni indispensabili rimanenti e mantenere i contatti così da indurle a cambiare la propria cultura, prevenendo ogni azione disperata di retroguardia che farebbe molte vittime.


Non scompariranno presto; dobbiamo continuare a parlare con loro o non cambieranno mai abbastanza da unirsi a noi…


“Abbiamo ancora bisogno di loro. Quando avevano il potere per poco non distruggevano il pianeta; ma fabbricano ancora delle parti importanti per la nostra infrastruttura. Loro pensano di aver bisogno di noi perché senza quelle esportazioni perderebbero la ragione d’esistere. In realtà, questo legame esile è la loro ultima possibilità. Ogni contatto serve a ricordare loro che c’è un’altra strada …

author: The Canadian Press
title: Tentative settlement in First Nation class action over non-consensual MRI scans
content:
A tentative settlement has been reached in a class action lawsuit alleging that members of

Pictou Landing First Nation

 in Nova Scotia underwent MRI scans without their consent.


The law firm representing the class confirmed Thursday that the proposed settlement with the defendants — two Halifax doctors — is subject to approval from the Nova Scotia Supreme Court.


None of the allegations in the lawsuit have been tested in court.


The original lawsuit, filed in 2020 and certified in 2024, alleged that radiologists Robert Miller and Sharon Clarke took magnetic resonance imaging scans of about 60 members of the Pictou Landing First Nation without their knowledge or consent.


A statement of claim filed in Nova Scotia Supreme Court says band members agreed to undergo the scans as part of a research project in 2017 but were subjected to additional “secret” scans of their livers for a separate study.


The lawsuit alleged the defendants were liable for invasion of privacy, acting recklessly and causing distress and anguish. They were also accused of negligence, unlawful imprisonment and assault and battery for allegedly keeping the participants inside the confined space of the MRI machine for longer than they should have.


The lawsuit also accused them of failing to advise participants of serious health issues that were discovered on the scans.


A lawyer representing the two doctors declined to comment on the proposed settlement.


The statement of claim also said former Chief Andrea Paul was among the Pictou Landing band members subjected to the MRIs.


“The MRI scans generated data that reveal intimate medical information about her body without her knowledge or consent,” the statement said. “She had been singled out for one reason — she was Mi’kmaq.”


It added that Paul felt she was discriminated against and that she suffered “a loss of dignity and self-esteem as a result.”


Read More: 


Pictou Landing First Nation members suing researchers for ‘secret’ experiment says claim


There is a long history of Indigenous people in Canada being subjected to medical treatment and research against their will, the lawsuit said.


Neither Paul nor the current chief of Pictou Landing First Nation, Tamara Young, were immediately available for comment.


A partner with the law firm said in a statement Thursday that the proposed $400,000 settlement would provide meaningful compensation to those who unknowingly participated in the study.


A hearing to approve the settlement is scheduled for Nov. 13.

Tentative settlement in First Nation class action over non-consensual MRI scans

APTN News

author: Luis Cosme Pinto
title: Melhor do mundo
content:
Faltam 28 minutos pro domingo virar segunda e o vagão só esvazia na estação Guilhermina-Esperança. O ambulante me cumprimenta com a cabeça, senta e acomoda a sacola preta entre as pernas. Estico o pescoço e vejo, lá dentro, algumas cocadas.


Parece que o dia foi bom, mesmo assim quero perguntar das vendas. Daria, com muito prazer, um pouco do meu tempo, do meu sono e até parte do que tenho na carteira para saber não só das cocadas. Quero conhecer, um tiquinho que seja, este trabalhador. Quem vende cocadas até o último trem do domingo tem muito pra contar.


Dou sorte. Mesmo tendo falado o dia inteiro de suas cocadas, que são gostosas, que desfazem na boca, que são baratas, que são mineiras e que vêm direto do Vale do Jequitinhonha, ele ainda quer falar.


Ajeita o boné, pigarreia.


— Meu nome é Getúlio. Getúlio Pereira da Silva. G. P. S. Nunca me perco. Entendeu? (rimos os dois) Mas sou conhecido como Raimundo. Eu explico: Pro ambulante, o marketing é tudo. Entro no vagão e anuncio: “Chegou a melhor cocada do mundo, a cocada do Raimundo”. Eu experimentei essa publicidade porque a rima é boa e eu sempre adorei o nome Raimundo. Tem passageiro que comenta. “Olha aí o Raimundo”. Então, deixa ficar. Virei Raimundo. Quer provar uma? É de graça que hoje esvaziei a sacola três vezes.


Aceito e me delicio com a doce mistura de coco e rapadura.


— Cremosa, né?


— Maravilhosa, Raimundo. Respondo com a boca ainda cheia e uma lasca de coco entre os dentes.


— Tem uns que reclamam da confusão. A gente grita mesmo. O jogador não pede a bola? O motoboy não buzina? O feirante não zoa? Por que a gente não pode? Ninguém é obrigado a saber da vida dos outros, mas será que eles sabem que, por trás de uma cocada, tem uma criança com fome, às vezes doente? Que tem aluguel, um monte de boletos, agiota te ameaçando?


— Quantos filhos você tem?


— Três. Olha aqui no celular. Anderson, Henrique e a caçula, a Marcela.


— Eu não peço nada, eu ofereço. Quem quer, quer. Quem não quer, não quer.


— Muita gente compra?


— Compra. E sabe por quê?


— Por quê?


— Porque o produto é bom e barato. E tem mais (ele sussurra): pobre não tem medo de gastar. Ele me vê e pensa: amanhã eu posso tá desempregado, posso ter que trabalhar como camelô. Então, eu ajudo agora e, se depois eu tiver no sufoco, alguém vai dar uma força.


— Mas dizem que é barato porque é clandestino.


— Mentira. É barato porque não tem intermediário; no supermercado o preço é maior porque eles têm muito mais despesas e também querem mais lucro. Aqui é diferente, vou no depósito e pago à vista.


— Então, por que é proibido?


— Porque é fácil mexer com o pobre. Eu garanto pro senhor. Meu produto não deve nada ao do supermercado. Eu ando de metrô e de trem todo dia e pago a passagem, viu? Eu sou camelô e passageiro ao mesmo tempo e garanto: a gente não atrapalha ninguém. Sabe o que atrapalha?


— O quê?


— O

atraso e a superlotação

. Tem que botar mais trens para circular. Só que a empresa ou o governo não quer gastar. É simples: com o trem cheio ganham mais. Agora, com a privatização, o que já era ruim ficou pior. Os vigilantes vêm pra cima como se o camelô fosse um bandido. Eu não sou bandido, sou empreendedor.


— Você manda bem, Raimundo. Já tinha falado de marketing, publicidade, agora empreendedor.


— Estudei um pouco. Empreendedor, eu ouvi essa no tempo que tinha passeata, sindicato. Durante um protesto, um cara subiu no caminhão e disse bem assim: Camelô é empreendedor e empreendedor é quem faz o Brasil crescer, nunca esqueci.


— Já tomaram sua mercadoria?


— Já, mas não desanimo. Toda profissão tem risco e eu adoro esse meu trabalho. Só que as autoridades não dão valor. Eles podiam cadastrar a gente.


— Como seria?


— Um número certo de ambulantes em cada trem, todo mundo com crachá, uniforme. Trabalho organizado.


Última estação. Getúlio levanta e me olha.


— Ué, não vai descer?


— Vou voltar. Vim até aqui para te ouvir.


A porta fecha e a gente acena um pro outro.


A voz feminina se impõe.


— Diamante Negro na promoção: é 3 por 5, que eu não brinco.

author: Administrador
title: Anomalías y Normalidades
content:
Ustedes saben, hay una serie de evidencias o de manuales que se heredan de generación en generación: Por ejemplo: el clásico “no eres tú, soy yo” en las rupturas amorosas; el “¿qué te hago si lo encuentro?” y el “Ponte el suéter”, de las mamaces; el “los extraterrestres se llevaron mi tarea, por diosito santo maestra” de estudiantes de todos los niveles.

Incluso hay la leyenda urbana de que esas frases están en un manual que se distribuye clandestinamente en madres, jóvenes y la niñez. En algún momento, todos los seres urbanos, acceden a esos manuales y sufren después lo que se llama “amnesia selectiva”, la que consiste, grosso modo, en que se nos olvida lo que no nos conviene, y recordamos sólo lo que nos favorece.

Pero en política están los manuales de qué hacer. Hasta hay un libro, que se estudia en la izquierda y en la derecha, que se llama así: “El Qué Hacer”. Hay también manuales de cómo hablar en público, influir en las personas, manejo de la imagen, cómo ser popular en las redes sociales y en las presidencias de las repúblicas.

Para que me entiendan, los manuales vienen siendo la versión prehistórica de los tutoriales.

Por encima, debajo y dentro de los manuales y tutoriales, están las evidencias. Valores y valoraciones que son incuestionables, están ahí y producen efectos en la vida cotidiana.

Estas evidencias son cuestionadas en tiempos de crisis por seres indefinibles (o también indefendibles o impronunciables) y, a veces, también son derrotadas… pero sólo en apariencia.

Por ejemplo, evidencias tales como “los varones son superiores a las hembras”; o “lo heterosexual es la normalidad y lo diferente es anormal, enfermo, despreciable, perseguible”; o “los indígenas son pueblos atrasados culturalmente y esperan con ansias ser rescatados para la civilización”. Estas evidencias difícilmente se manifestarán en palabras y en público en estos tiempos. Pero siguen produciendo sus efectos en la vida cotidiana, en los programas de gobiernos, en estatutos partidarios, en líneas editoriales, en reality shows como las mañaneras, en redes sociales.

Pero en el quehacer político hay dos evidencias que, como todas las evidencias, son naturales, normales, eternas:

Una es que es las injusticias se combaten desde arriba y, en consecuencia, desde arriba se construye la justicia.

Otra es que es posible cambiar las cosas desde dentro.

Como ahí es donde se ubica el núcleo, el nudo gordiano de la política, entonces se combinan: desde dentro y desde arriba, se nos dice. “Hacemos política para llegar al Poder y, desde allá arriba, resolver todos los problemas”.

Y así se construyen toda clase de coartadas. En la biblioteca de babel de las inexistentes ciencias políticas se reciclan bestsellers o aparecen nuevos que, en realidad, no son sino refritos de los antiguos, y aparece una camada de iniciados, los nuevos especialistas no en explicar la realidad, sino en construir coartadas a cuál más de ridícula.

Así desaparecen y reaparecen Keynes, Marx, Lenin, Trotsky, Mao.

Es evidente, se dicen y nos dicen, que sólo desde arriba y desde dentro de pueden cambiar las cosas. Por eso, ése debe ser el destino de todas las revoluciones, movilizaciones, acciones políticas.

Se construyen así partidos políticos, programas de acción, cambios verdaderos, dogmas ideológicos, páginas editoriales, conferencias magistrales, viajes con todo pagado al paraíso soñado en turno (China está de moda y modo ahora); ediciones de la historia para que los cercanos sean los protagonistas, y no quienes pusieron el cuerpo y el alma en la lucha.

Aquí hay que reconocer que la religión, a diferencia de las doctrinas políticas, es la única que reconoce y explicita que sus dogmas son dogmas: dogmas de fe, nos dicen. La religión es más honesta que cualquier propuesta ideológica.

La política no. Disfraza sus dogmas de análisis científicos. De serios estudios, de cantidad de notas de pie de página, de popularidad evidente. Por eso resulta que la Inteligencia Artificial no es tan inteligente, porque ha sido creada a la imagen y semejanza del Dominus, el señor, el mandón.

Repetir, hasta el eructo, las evidencias, es la consigna. Por eso es tan impopular el pensamiento crítico cuando es eso, es decir, crítico.

Porque en todos los monasterios de la política realista, el cuestionamiento es herejía y blasfemia. Y si no hay crucifijos de madera es porque para eso están las redes sociales, a quienes los medios de comunicación tradicional envidian ahora su papel de …

author: Gladys Stagno
title: Quién es Brad Parscale, el gurú de la ultraderecha y mentor de Cerimedo
content:
De Trump al ecosistema libertario: una trama que conecta campañas electorales, bases de datos, inteligencia artificial y operadores de la nueva derecha latinoamericana. El recorrido de Cerimedo, la punta del ovillo.


Por Gladys Stagno


El 10 de febrero pasado, en el club Mar-a-Lago de Donald Trump, Florida, la crème de la ultraderecha latina celebró la Hispanic Prosperity Gala, un evento privado al que asisten líderes empresariales, políticos y figuras varias con nexos en Estados Unidos. Entre ellos estuvo Fernando Cerimedo, quien fue premiado como “Consultor Político Hispano del Año”.


Luego de recibir el trofeo vidriado de manos de Eduardo Bolsonaro (hijo de Jair y exiliado en Estados Unidos desde el año pasado), el exasesor de Javier Milei y fundador de

La Derecha Diario

 aprovechó para agradecer a sus colaboradores en español y en inglés. Las gracias anglosajonas tuvieron un destinatario: Brad Parscale, su mentor.


Esa historia podría haber quedado olvidada en el mar de premios endogámicos del espacio, si no fuera porque en agosto Cerimedo fue arrestado en Bolivia, acusado de intento de femicidio, violencia doméstica y —allanamientos mediante— enriquecimiento ilícito. Y así, la noticia que lo llevó a las tapas de los diarios también ofició de punta del ovillo para desenredar el entramado de articulación internacional de la ultraderecha en América Latina, que tiene a Parscale como estratega central.


El mentor de la comunicación ultra


Los antecedentes de Brad Parscale se remontan a comienzos de 2015, cuando meses antes de que Donald Trump anunciara su candidatura a la Presidencia de Estados Unidos, creó el sitio web de la campaña en dos días.


Para 2016, este ingeniero de la comunicación política ya era director de medios digitales del futuro presidente, y un par de años después —con Trump ya asumido— era nombrado jefe de campaña para su reelección en 2020.


Bajo ese paraguas, Parscale construyó Campaign Nucleus, un motor de gestión de relaciones (CRM) integrado con bases de datos de votantes, capacidades de segmentación y automatización de mensajería política directa. Dicho fácil: la particularidad de su plataforma es su capacidad para centralizar, segmentar y automatizar la difusión de narrativas políticas en medios tradicionales y digitales.


Según cuenta un informe del Registro de Ataques de la Derecha Radicalizada (RADAR) difundido por

Agencia Áncora

, en agosto de 2017, una empresa llamada CloudCommerce adquirió los activos comerciales de Parscale por 9 millones de dólares en acciones preferentes. Luego de eso, Parscale se unió a su junta directiva y se convirtió en el principal accionista.


En febrero de 2018, CloudCommerce creó una subsidiaria llamada Data Propria: una empresa de análisis de datos y ciencia conductual fundada por exintegrantes de la consultora británica Cambridge Analytica. Si bien un mes después estalló el escándalo que desnudó que esta última utilizó datos personales de más de 50 millones de usuarios de Facebook para crear campañas políticas sucias en distintos países, Data Propria casi no fue investigada.


La presunta objetividad de la IA


Luego de pasar bajo el radar, CloudCommerce cambió de marca y se convirtió en AiAdvertising. Y bajo ese nombre diseñó una plataforma para gestionar “personas” sintéticas generadas por IA, que permiten la predicción del comportamiento de audiencia sin depender del rastreo individual tradicional.


Parscale también se volvió el impulsor de la estrategia conocida como framing o “contaminación sintáctica”, para moldear cómo los modelos de lenguaje de IA (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) responden a ciertas preguntas.


En concreto, la misma consiste en incidir en las búsquedas de los chatbots con material prefabricado para un determinado objetivo. Así, como los grandes modelos de lenguaje extraen su conocimiento del rastreo continuo de la Web abierta, la infraestructura digital de Parscale diseña a gran escala portales con determinadas características —estructuras sintácticas repetitivas, tono sobrio, aparente rigor académico— que condicionan los resultados y generan una respuesta tendenciosa, disfrazada de ecuánime.


El ejemplo que ofrece RADAR es el trabajo que el operador digital realizó luego de firmar un contrato de 9 millones de dólares con la Cancillería israelí para mejorar la imagen pública de ese país en la base social del movimiento MAGA.
