title: Louise Michel - Sobre las mujeres
content:
Autor/a

: Louise Michel

Título

: Sobre las mujeres

Fecha

: 1886

Notas

: Extracto de la obra original

Mémoires de Louise Michel, écrits par elle-même

, 1886 (Chapitre IX). Traducido y editado en octubre de 2026 por

La Conquista del Panda

 bajo licencia

CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

Fuente

: Recuperado en septiembre de 2026 desde

Panarchy


 El ser, al igual que la especie

[1]

, crece y florece en hojas y flores. Al igual que los frutos verdes, solo serviremos para abonar la tierra, pero quienes vengan después de nosotros llevarán la semilla de la justicia y la libertad.


 La savia que asciende, en nuestra época de transición, es poderosa. De los cruces humanos de hoy, a través de infinitas vicisitudes, solo pueden nacer especies revolucionarias, incluso entre aquellos que niegan la inminencia de la Revolución.


 La lenta evolución ha llegado a su fin; es necesario que la crisálida rompa la vieja piel; eso es la Revolución.


 Desde que la humanidad yace con las alas envueltas, han germinado nuevos sentidos; incluso físicamente, el nuevo ser humano ya no se nos parecerá.


 Muramos, pues, miserables como somos, y que se derrumben sobre nosotros nuestros monstruosos errores, hasta el último; y que la especie humana se despliegue y viva allí donde se degollaba al rebaño humano.


 Salve a la humanidad libre y fuerte que no comprenderá cómo durante tanto tiempo hemos vegetado como nuestros antepasados de las cavernas, ya sin devorarnos la carne unos a otros (ya no somos lo bastante fuertes), pero devorándonos la vida.


 ¿Acaso hoy en día las multitudes no se hunden en hecatombes y miserias incontables para el mero placer de unos pocos, con la única diferencia respecto a la época de nuestros antepasados de que ahora es a mayor escala?


 ¿Acaso no se segaban los pueblos como si fueran cosechas? Al segar los rastrojos, se sacude el grano sobre la tierra para la primavera secular; cada gota de sangre de los cruces humanos hierve en nuestras venas; es en esta tormenta donde surgirá la renovación.


 Si la Revolución que retumba bajo la tierra dejara algo del viejo mundo, ¡habría que volver a empezar desde cero! Por lo tanto, la vieja piel de la crisálida humana desaparecerá para siempre. La mariposa debe desplegar sus alas, salir sangrando de su prisión o perecer.


 ¡Salve a la especie de sangre caliente y rubicunda en la que todo será justicia, armonía, fuerza y luz!


 En aquellos tiempos, se tomará siempre el camino recto en lugar de buscar millones de desvíos, y los pequeños destellos titilantes que se confunden con estrellas, y que apenas son luciérnagas, desaparecerán en la claridad del día.


 ¡Qué debacle, amigos míos, en todas esas viejas cajas de errores! Seremos barridos por ese polvo; intentemos al menos que sea de la forma menos estúpida posible.


 He visto allí, en los bosques de Caledonia, derrumbarse de repente, con un suave crujido de tronco podrido, viejos niaulíes que habían vivido su cuasi eternidad como árboles. Cuando el remolino de polvo desapareció, solo quedó un montón de cenizas sobre el que, como coronas de cementerio, yacen ramas verdes: los últimos brotes del viejo árbol, arrastrados por el resto. Las miríadas de insectos que se multiplicaban allí desde hacía siglos quedan sepultados bajo el derrumbe. Algunos, removiendo con dificultad las cenizas, contemplan, asombrados e inquietos, la luz del día que los mata; sus especies, nacidas en la sombra, no soportarán la luz. Así, habitamos el viejo árbol social, que nos empeñamos en creer muy vivo, mientras que el más mínimo soplo lo aniquilará y dispersará sus cenizas.


 Ningún ser escapa a las transformaciones que, al cabo de unos años, lo han cambiado hasta la última partícula. Luego llega la Revolución, que lo sacude todo con sus tormentas.


 ¡Ahí es donde nos encontramos! Los seres, las especies y, dentro de las especies, esas dos partes de la humanidad: el hombre y la mujer, que deberían caminar de la mano y cuyo antagonismo perdurará mientras la más fuerte mande o crea mandar sobre la otra, reducida a las artimañas y al dominio oculto, que son las armas de los esclavos. Por todas partes se libra la lucha.


 Si se reconociera la igualdad entre ambos sexos, sería una brecha notable en la estupidez humana. Mientras tanto, la mujer sigue siendo, como decía el viejo Molière, el caldo del hombre. El sexo fuerte llega incluso a halagar al otro calificándolo de «bello sexo».


 Hace ya mucho tiempo que acabamos con esa «fuerza», y somos …

author: Redazione_web
title: “La mia famiglia è in carcere”. Turchia: repressione e resistenza dei movimenti LGBTQIAP+
content:
Nella notte tra il 12 e il 13 settembre la polizia turca entra nelle case dellə attivistə, perquisisce le sedi delle associazioni LGBTQIAP+, sequestra telefoni e computer, fa irruzione nei locali. L’operazione si estende a quindici province, coinvolge 162 persone, nove associazioni e tredici attività. Contemporaneamente viene oscurata una parte consistente dello spazio digitale del movimento: siti delle associazioni, media, account di attivistə, avvocatə e gruppi universitari.


Nel rastrellamento vengono messe insieme realtà molto diverse: organizzazioni storiche e riconosciute internazionalmente come Kaos GL, associazioni impegnate sull’HIV, ma anche locali e luoghi della socialità e della sessualità queer. Le indagini insistono su sex work, sostanze, «oscenità» e altre ipotesi di reato. Attivistə turche con cui siamo in contatto leggono questa sovrapposizione come una precisa strategia di legittimazione della repressione davanti all’opinione pubblica: associare il movimento LGBTQIAP+ a droga, prostituzione e criminalità permette di presentare il rastrellamento non come un attacco politico alle sue strutture organizzate, ma come un’operazione a difesa della società, dei bambini e della famiglia. Una lettura che trova riscontro nello stesso linguaggio delle autorità: la Procura parla della necessità di impedire la «normalizzazione» di queste pratiche agli occhi della società, mentre il Ministero della Giustizia richiama insieme protezione dei minori, famiglia e «valori morali comuni». Il governo chiama l’operazione Ailem Güvende, “La mia famiglia è al sicuro”.


Il nome non è un dettaglio propagandistico. Dice molto di quello che sta succedendo in Turchia e, insieme, di un’offensiva reazionaria che conosciamo bene anche da questa parte d’Europa. La famiglia da difendere, i bambini da salvare, la denatalità, la “natura”, la “morale”, il gender e le persone queer e trans trasformate in una minaccia: sono parole che viaggiano da anni attraverso confini, destre, governi e movimenti anti-gender. In Turchia questa grammatica politica è diventata progressivamente politica di Stato.


La repressione del movimento viene da lontano. A Istanbul il Pride viene vietato ogni anno dal 2015, ma ogni anno il movimento prova comunque a riprendersi le strade. Divieti analoghi colpiscono Pride e iniziative LGBTQIAP+ anche in altre città e la risposta è diventata quasi rituale: cordoni di polizia, cortei dispersi, violenze e fermi. Ancora nel giugno scorso, il 24° Istanbul Pride si è tenuto a Kadıköy nonostante il divieto: 65 persone sono state fermate. Nello stesso Pride Month ci sono stati altri fermi a İzmir, Ankara e durante il Trans Pride di Istanbul. Non è quindi la presenza LGBTQIAP+ nello spazio pubblico a essere scomparsa: è diventato sempre più alto il prezzo da pagare per renderla visibile.


La svolta familista dell’attuale fase ha però un passaggio fondamentale nel 2021, quando Erdoğan ritira la Turchia dalla Convenzione di Istanbul contro la violenza sulle donne. Il governo lega apertamente quella scelta all’omosessualità, sostenendo che la Convenzione sia stata utilizzata per «normalizzarla» a danno dei valori sociali e familiari. Non è casuale che l’attacco ai diritti delle donne e quello alle persone LGBTQIAP+ si incontrino proprio qui. La famiglia viene costruita come un corpo sotto assedio, da proteggere contemporaneamente dal femminismo, dall’autodeterminazione delle donne, dalle soggettività queer e trans e da tutto ciò che incrina la naturalizzazione dei ruoli di genere.


È una costruzione che negli anni successivi diventa sempre più organica. Le campagne contro la cosiddetta “propaganda LGBT” si intrecciano con le proposte per costituzionalizzare il matrimonio eterosessuale, le politiche pronataliste e l’attacco ai percorsi di affermazione di genere. Nel 2024 arriva un passaggio decisivo: con il Family Protection and Strengthening Vision Document and Action Plan 2024–2028 la protezione e il rafforzamento della famiglia diventano un programma pluriennale dello Stato, articolato in cinque obiettivi strategici, quindici target e cento azioni e affidato a organismi nazionali e provinciali. Seguono l’“Anno della famiglia” nel 2025 e, quest’anno, il lancio del “Decennio della famiglia e della popolazione 2026–2035”.


Il collegamento con quello che sta accadendo oggi non dobbiamo costruirlo noi: è lo stesso ministro della Giustizia Akın Gürlek a collocare l’operazione “Ailem Güvende” dentro questa politica. La …

author: Maríangeles Guerrero
title: “Debemos pensar en una insurrección popular frente a los gobiernos fascistas”
content:
Por Mariángeles Guerrero


María Leonor Yonda es vicepresidenta del Coordinador Nacional Agrario (CNA) de Colombia. El CNA comenzó como un proceso de base en 2009; hoy nuclea a 50 organizaciones conformadas por jóvenes, campesinos y campesinas, pescadores y pescadoras y pueblos negros e indígenas de ese país. Tiene presencia en 24 de los 32 departamentos de Colombia y fue impulsora de los Territorios Agrarios Campesinos (Tecam), reconocidos por el gobierno de Gustavo Petro en 2024. El nuevo gobierno, de Abelardo de la Espriella, promete alianzas con los sectores concentrados de la economía y el recrudecimiento de la persecución a lideresas y líderes campesinos. Ante ese panorama,

“proponemos un modelo de vida opuesto al de la clase dominante, que ha ostentado el poder bajo la criminalización, con fuerzas como el paramilitarismo”

, asegura Yonda.


Entre las reivindicaciones del CNA están

 la recuperación y la permanencia en la tierra, la defensa del territorio y el ambiente, la agroecología, la soberanía alimentaria y la defensa de los derechos humanos

, a los que prefieren definir como

 “derechos de los pueblos”

. Es, en términos de la entrevistada, “una estrategia de lucha de clases, frente al capitalismo, al despojo y al extractivismo”.


Respecto a la injerencia estadounidense en América Latina, denunciada por observadores internacionales respecto a Honduras, Colombia y Argentina (por dar algunos ejemplos), reflexiona: “

No somos el patio trasero de Estados Unidos, somos la puerta delantera.

 Por eso es esta guerra mediática, esta narrativa que viene ganando el fascismo. Tenemos que poner nuestra inteligencia al servicio del movimiento social, cambiar la disputa ideológica y ser más ágiles en la comunicación. Los pueblos nos tenemos que juntar para cambiar esa batalla desde lo ideológico, desde la formación y desde lo organizativo”.


Las raíces del CNA se remontan al paro cafetero de 1997 llevado adelante en el centro del país, entre otros motivos, por las deudas que asediaban a los productores de café. En la memoria se inscriben además las movilizaciones de trabajadores caficultores del 2013-2014. La organización también encuentra su raigambre en la Asociación Nacional de Usuarios Campesinos, una de las primeras organizaciones campesinas colombianas, que data de los años 60. “Venimos de ese legado. Muchos padres y familias hacían parte de la Asociación y desde ahí surgimos”, afirma.


Oriunda de El Tambo y Argelia (localidad del Cauca, en el oeste de Colombia), explica que la apuesta política del Coordinador se enmarca en el internacionalismo, por eso confluyen en La Vía Campesina. La formación política del CNA tiene componentes de geopolítica y pone la lupa sobre cómo el imperialismo fue parte de la estrategia de guerra interna en Colombia, conflicto armado que lleva décadas y que intentó resolverse mediante el Acuerdo de Paz de 2016.


Según Yonda, el eje de acción prioritario del CNA

 es la movilización constante y la recuperación de tierras frente a las empresas que históricamente han despojado al campesinado

. En Colombia, para 2022, el uno por ciento de la población concentraba el 81 por ciento de la tierra, según Oxfam.


Foto: Coordinador Nacional Agrario de Colombia


El campesino: una identidad política negada, una palabra prohibida


El Estado colombiano firmó, en 2016, un Acuerdo de Paz con las Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia (FARC). Implicaba la deposición de las armas por parte de la guerrilla, pero también el compromiso estatal con reformas estructurales y políticas que mejoren las condiciones de vida en las zonas rurales, donde las FARC emergieron y tuvieron su mayor desarrollo. Entre los puntos del acuerdo, una de las claves era

la democratización de la tierra: la reforma agraria

.


El gobierno de Gustavo Petro (2022-2026) fue el que más avanzó respecto a la cantidad de hectáreas devueltas a las familias campesinas. Según la

Agencia Nacional de Tierras

, el ex presidente Juan Manuel Santos entregó 27.287 hectáreas e Iván Duque 32.614. Hasta fines de 2025, el gobierno de Gustavo Petro había gestionado la entrega de 700.000.


Si bien los crímenes contra líderes campesinos ocurrieron en todos los gobiernos, según datos del Instituto de Estudios para el Desarrollo y la Paz (Indepaz), desde que De la Espriella ganó las elecciones se registraron 61 campesinas, campesinos e indígenas asesinados. Por ejemplo, el 31 de agosto

fueron asesinados la lideresa indígena María …

title: Día de Acción Global por el acceso al Aborto Legal y Seguro
content:
Ante el Congreso de la Nación, colectivas y activistas feministas se manifestaron “para defender el derecho a decidir, el acceso a la salud sexual y reproductiva, la Educación Sexual Integral y todos los derechos conquistados gracias a nuestra lucha”.

Bajo la consigna “Educación sexual para decidir, anticonceptivos para no abortar y aborto legal para no morir”, la Campaña Nacional por el Derecho al Aborto Legal, Seguro y Gratuito junto a otras organizaciones y activistas realizó un pañuelazo en la Plaza del Congreso, denunciando el “vaciamiento sistemático de las políticas de salud sexual y (no) reproductiva” por parte del gobierno nacional de ultraderecha de Javier Milei.


Desde hace más de tres décadas, el 28 de septiembre se conmemora el Día de Acción Global por el Aborto Legal, una fecha que nació en América Latina y que cada año reactualiza la consigna por el derecho a decidir. Su origen se encuentra en 1990, cuando durante el V Encuentro Feminista Latinoamericano y del Caribe realizado en San Bernardo,  activistas de toda la región declararon el 28 de septiembre como Día por la Despenalización y Legalización del Aborto, a partir de una propuesta de la delegación brasileña que recuperó un antecedente histórico: ese mismo día de 1871, Brasil promulgó la Ley de Libertad de Vientres, que liberaba a los hijos de mujeres esclavizadas.


La sanción de la Ley 27.610 en 2020 convirtió a Argentina en referencia regional: la norma garantiza la Interrupción Voluntaria del Embarazo hasta la semana 14 y la Interrupción Legal del Embarazo en casos de violación o riesgo para la salud. Sin embargo, las organizaciones que convocan a la movilización advierten que, si bien la ley continúa vigente, el acceso efectivo al aborto enfrenta problemas de financiamiento, provisión de medicamentos y desigualdades territoriales. Entre las dificultades señaladas figuran recortes en políticas de salud sexual, dificultades en la provisión de anticonceptivos y medicamentos como misoprostol y mifepristona, y retrocesos en programas como el Plan ENIA.


En ese marco político, el presidente Milei volvió a atacar al feminismo y al aborto legal: frente a su público favorito, empresarios, responsabilizó a los sectores que impulsaron la legalización por la caída en la tasa de natalidad.


Desde las organizaciones feministas y sectores académicos se responde que la baja de la natalidad no se explica por la interrupción del embarazo, sino por causas económicas y sociales como la precarización laboral, la falta de vivienda y la sobrecarga de cuidados.

author: Unknown
title: Rencontre avec Sandeep Bakshi sur Frontières queer
content:
Jeudi 15 octobre à 19h30, rencontre avec Sandeep Bakshi pour la sortie de son livre Frontières queer, sexualité, colonialité, décolonialité. La rencontre sera animée par Zaid du collectif sud-asiatique/Brown antiraciste.


Le queer est-il seulement occidental

 

? Conçu au cœur même des Empires, son lexique est-il utile loin des métropoles et logiques coloniales

 

? Dans cet ouvrage, Sandeep Bakshi remet en question les généalogies admises du queer pour échapper aux instrumentalisations et aux normalisations dont il est l'objet.


Partant de pratiques et d'analyses des Suds, ce livre montre que, si les études et le militantisme queer ont produit des formes de pensée radicales, elles ne sont pas immunisées contre les a priori culturels, sociaux et raciaux. Le queer, lui aussi, a sa colonialité. Dès lors, c'est en adoptant une perspective décoloniale que le queer retrouvera toute la vigueur de son insurrection initiale, pour semer à nouveau le trouble.

author: Progressive International
title: From Law to Justice
content:
As Trump attacked the ICC and Netanyahu faced a walkout at the UN, forty states gathered to put an arms embargo, protections for the Court and a new UN mechanism modelled on the Special Committee against Apartheid.

Last week, the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) counted what remained of Gaza’s economy after almost three years of genocide and almost two decades of siege. Ninety-two per cent of its economic establishments have been damaged or destroyed. Unemployment has reached 78 per cent. GDP per person fell to $212 last year — barely 17 per cent of its pre-genocide level — while less than 1.5 per cent of Gaza’s cropland remains accessible and undamaged. Recovery and reconstruction will cost at least $71.5 billion. Pedro Manuel Moreno, acting head of UNCTAD, called it “the world’s most severe economic crisis on record”.

These were the conditions in which the governments of the world assembled in New York for the 81st United Nations General Assembly. On Monday 21 September, a thousand gathered at Riverside Church to celebrate the Charter on which the institution was founded, hosted by South Africa. Martin Luther King Jr stood in the same church in 1967 to deliver Beyond Vietnam. Nelson Mandela came there four months after his release from prison and thanked the movements that had sustained sanctions against apartheid — before urging them to keep up the pressure until victory was secured. “We acted because we know what global solidarity can do,” South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola told the gathering. The Hague Group, he said, embodies a “shared conviction that concrete action is needed.”

A day later, Donald Trump used the General Assembly podium to attack the International Criminal Court. He called it an “evil” and “rogue institution” and urged its 125 member states to withdraw. His administration has already imposed financial sanctions and visa restrictions on ICC officials and threatened further measures that could stifle the Court’s ability to operate. Trump has said the campaign is aimed at protecting Benjamin Netanyahu, for whom the Court issued an arrest warrant in 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.

On Thursday, Netanyahu himself took the same podium. Dozens of delegates walked out as he began speaking. He held aloft a pager, invoking Israel’s 2024 terror attack in Lebanon: “Remember the beepers? Hezbollah certainly remembers them.”

Netanyahu denied that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, denounced his critics as “moral cowards” and praised Trump as Israel’s greatest partner. Outside the UN, protesters blocked streets demanding an end to US arms supplies to Israel; at least 30 were arrested.

By Friday morning, another gathering was underway inside UN headquarters. In the Trusteeship Council Chamber, once at the centre of the UN’s work of decolonisation, forty states — represented by foreign ministers and senior diplomats — joined The Hague Group’s largest meeting yet, co-sponsored by South Africa and Malaysia in defence of international law.

Minister Lamola opened by recalling the machinery built against apartheid: the UN Special Committee established in 1962 to monitor and organise international action, followed by the campaign that turned a voluntary arms embargo into a mandatory Security Council measure in 1977. The Hague Group itself had begun with nine states in January 2025. “Our task today,” Lamola told the room, “is to turn concern into compliance, and law into protection.”

The states gathered in New York discussed a series of concrete proposals. One would create a new UN mechanism drawing on the Special Committee against Apartheid to monitor compliance with international law and coordinate action between states. Another would continue efforts for a Security Council arms embargo on Israel. For the ICC, states discussed blocking statutes against sanctions on the Court, measures to keep it operating under pressure, and coordinated action to protect judges and prosecutors from retaliation. Norway pledged to work on the Court’s “business continuity”, while other interventions stressed cooperation to ensure that its decisions can still be carried out. South Africa and Malaysia committed to continue consultations with participating governments on how to put the proposals into practice.

“The law is clear,” Indonesia’s representative told the room. “Our challenge now is to give it practical consequence.” That same week, UNCTAD had …

author: Laura Hernández
title: Clinton-Era Laws Passed 30 Years Ago Enabled Trump’s Anti-Immigrant Agenda.
content:
Clinton’s ‘96 laws provided the legal foundation for mass detention, rapid deportations, and the evasion of due process.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The more the American public sees of President Donald Trump’s hardline, anti-immigrant policies in action — the deaths, military-style invasions of neighborhoods, and mass detention and deportations — the more his approval on the issue drops.

If this trend sounds familiar, it’s because a similar wave of disapproval played out in Trump’s first term. Despite that backlash, Trump returned to office embracing even more extreme measures.

We must finally confront and uproot the core of the U.S.’s anti-immigrant underbelly, which is largely reflected in the racially motivated notion of criminalization.

Trump was not the first politician to exploit the concept of criminality, and he certainly won’t be the last. Criminalizing narratives are deeply planted in the American psyche, and they have commonly acted as the vessel through which white supremacist rhetoric and policy are ingrained into our culture and laws.

In the late 1980’s, criminalization went mainstream in the form of racist dog whistles, particularly those hinging on vile anti-Blackness deployed by politicians seeking to activate white voters. In the decades since, conservative and liberal leaders alike more purposefully extended this criminality framework to immigration — so much so that it’s now perhaps the primary driver of the public immigration debate.

Consider how Americans of all political stripes are often presented with the binary choice of supporting the “right” type of immigrant. In this oversimplification, immigrants fall into categories like “good” or “bad,” “legal” or “illegal,” “deserving” or “undeserving.”

Trump did not invent these narratives. They’ve underpinned both major parties’ politics of immigration for several decades, despite their basis in fiction and fear-mongering rather than evidence and compassion, or the fact these narratives are weaponized against non-white immigrants who for centuries have disproportionately faced restrictive and punitive policies for the act of seeking relief in this country.

But Trump’s partisan opposition, despite its massive opportunities in the face of unpopular, hardline policies, has repeatedly failed to capture the public’s long-term support on immigration. Too often, Democrats repackage the same old criminalizing narratives — often in softer terms, but always in line with the oversimplified good-or-bad thinking. This lack of imagination is reflected in the nearly annual bipartisan votes to increase funding for federal enforcement agencies like Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection, as well as Democratic leaders’ messaging and policies.

Take, for example, former President Barack Obama’s push to deport “felons, not families”; Joe Biden squandering his mandate to reverse the cruelty of Trump’s first term by continuing many Trump policies, like Title 42 and the backing of for-profit immigrant detention; or Kamala Harris, in her presidential bid, focusing much of her immigration rhetoric on “securing” the border.

It’s a toxic cycle: The public rightfully disapproves of the atrocities of anti-immigrant policies; in response, liberals roll out unimaginative plans hinged on outdated narratives; and finally, in the vacuum created by the lack of any tangible, pro-immigrant vision, the right recaptures the public’s attention with fear mongering and a sensationalist focus on crime and the border.

To break this cycle, we must imagine a pro-immigrant future in which our communities, not politicians and pundits, get to define safety.

We can start with recognizing that the modern-day legal basis for the criminalization of immigrants largely rests on a pair of anti-immigrant bills signed into law by Bill Clinton 30 years ago. Building upon the U.S. legacy of racialized immigration control, the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (IIRIRA) and the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act (AEDPA) further entrenched mass incarceration and laid the blueprint for the detention and deportation machine we have today.

These laws drastically expanded the government’s ability to automatically detain and deport people without due process and without consideration for their current circumstances.

IIRIRA, in particular …

author: Clare Hymer
title: Who Does the Green Party’s ‘Zionism Is Racism’ Motion Really Serve?
content:
It’s Saturday morning in a Victorian public garden in Camden, north London, and the mood is upbeat. Green leader Zack Polanski is fighting a byelection in suboptimal conditions: in a seat with an 11,000 Labour majority, his approval ratings in a slump, and, unlike when the party won Gorton and Denton in February, a prime minister in Downing Street who not everyone totally hates. But on his side he has a party membership surpassing 230,000, of whom around 200 enthusiastic volunteers are out today. If Green members are apparently

“turning on” Polanski for not being anti-Zionist enough

, as one recent report in the rightwing press claimed, you can’t feel it here. 


But that’s not to say Zionism isn’t being talked about. It is, as much on this sunny morning in Holborn and St Pancras as in the media in recent weeks, because of a controversial motion titled ‘Zionism is Racism’, set to be debated at the party’s conference just days before the 8 October byelection.


The Greens already have strong policies on Israel and Palestine, describing Israeli conduct as apartheid and genocide, backing a full arms embargo, sanctions and an end to occupation and illegal settlements. But the Zionism is Racism motion takes things further. It calls on the party to, among other things, state that it is anti-Zionist, support a single, democratic Palestinian state, demand freedom for Palestinian political prisoners, oppose the Palestine Action ban, affirm Palestinians’ right to resistance, and, as per the title, equate Zionism with racism.


The motion itself isn’t new, and nor is the hoo-ha around it. Submitted to the party’s spring conference but not put to members due to time constraints (

or sabotage

, depending on who you ask), it was leapt on by the rightwing press as evidence of a Green antisemitism crisis. By avoiding debating the motion back in March, the party just kicked the can down the road, Novara Media reporter

Rivkah Brown wrote at the time

. But some think that a fight, both with the media and within the party, is exactly what’s needed.


“The whole point of this motion is for us to challenge and confront the establishment,”

said Lubna Speitan

, a British-Palestinian activist and the proposer of the motion. “It doesn’t matter what the leadership thinks… It’s about us, the members… forcing their hand.”


Speitan’s comments followed

an interview

 in which Polanski, who’s been under pressure to take a stance, said he was undecided about voting for the motion. He did say he believed it needed to better safeguard anti-Zionist Jews from being accused of racism, and it should be up to the people of the region to determine their own political settlement, not the Green party of England and Wales or the British state. Still, on Thursday night, Polanski sat in front of the Board of Deputies of British Jews and declared he was an anti-Zionist – something supporters of the motion

claimed as a win

.


Ashok Kumar, a Green member who’s backing the motion, told Novara Media: “It’s the right position”.


“[The] politics of the country have shifted quite dramatically since late 2023,” Kumar said. “We’re actually meeting the proportion of the population that really feels strongly about this.


“There is no fence-sitting on this… Some things aren’t nuanced. Slavery, not nuanced. Zionism, not nuanced… The point is to throw down the gauntlet and say, ‘You’re either with the people of Palestine, or you’re with the oppressors’.” 


But even anti-Zionist members who don’t find much to disagree with in the content of the motion have raised doubts about whether or not it’s strategic. Some activists are dismissive of the media ire it’s drawing: “Come at us,” said Kumar, “You stand up to the press… and people actually respect that.” But others believe a big debate about Zionism could harm the party’s electoral chances – and without doing anything to make Palestinians’ lives any better. 


“It’s quite an abstract debate, it’s quite an academic debate”, said a local party chair, who asked to remain anonymous due to his role. “It’s not particularly relevant for most people in the country at large.”


A Green councillor in south London agreed. “[The motion] traps us at the level of language and definitions… There’s a perception that there’s a dial called ‘anti-Zionism’ and the higher you turn it, the more Palestinian liberation you get. And obviously that’s not true.”

author: Ishita Chakrabarty
title: Hindus for Human Rights: ‘Racism is not just about violence, it manifests through misinformation’
content:
To all those who have come from far off-lands and continents; who have made it here despite the monumental barriers that passport privilege poses for some over others — the intense questioning as to motivation; the demand for return tickets; the visa costs that keep escalating year on year; the bank statements and medical reports to prove you will not become a burden onto the system, I am one among you.

To those who have lived here for generations and are yet still told to “Go back where you came from”.

To those who hold a sacred relationship to this land — whose belonging to this land can never be severed by the operation of an unjust, extractive and foreign imposed law.

And to all those who join us here in solidarity, who believe in the idea of an inclusive, egalitarian and multicultural Australia.

I come from Bengal in India. I am representing Hindus for Human Rights, a voice for progressive Hindus and Indians working for inter-faith and inter-community respect and understanding and advocating against all kinds of discrimination and bigotry.

Coming from India, I know all too well what hate, bigotry and the belief of the superiority of some over the other looks like, and how the destruction of the very fabric of society is tantamount to the destruction of the human within us.

It is because of the love I hold towards my home country and the appreciation for being here that I believe we must join hands in the fight against racism and bigotry, whether it comes from the far right politics of One Nation, or from the Hindutva ideology that considers Dalits, Muslims, Christians and other minorities inferior and less than human.

As I speak, Muslims are being lynched, evicted, legally stripped of their citizenship through complicit state institutions. Christians are being hounded, their prayer services are being stopped mid-worship on allegations of forced conversions. Dalits and other caste minorities remain trapped in a system where the so-called upper castes get offended by someone for sporting a moustache, or a Dalit man “daring” to attend their own wedding on horseback.

As a person bearing a majoritarian identity, I feel even more compelled to not only speak of racism emanating from a certain and distant political entity, but also the hatred, transpiring within our own South Asian community, including in Australia.

Identities, beliefs and practices travel alongside communities and are often seen through acts such as questioning one’s food preferences, tasking that one Indian student whose identity is given away by their surname to undertake the menial tasks in the house, through casual bullying. They perpetrate through closed social groups and in marriage alliances.

Hindus for Human Rights along with allies have worked hard and successfully to have caste discrimination included as a form of racism in city councils and universities.

When we speak of racism and bigotry it is also important to speak about these internal exclusions that we have created. For the same hatred that I mentioned earlier is then taken and twisted to justify that the far right is not against all immigrants — only the “bad ones” who refuse to “assimilate”, for example, the hijab- or turban-wearing student of Indian origin.

It is used to legitimise the exclusion of our fellow community members, as when One Nation leader Pauline Hanson keeps speaking of how Indians are the “good, hardworking migrants”.

It is seen when platforms show her attending Diwali festivals and being warmly received by diasporic Indians, represented through associations like the Hindu Council of Australia, or when she visits that one Indian migrant-run shop in Townsville, posing with the owner while eating fish and chips.

When I speak of racism, I speak of the overt acts: The people who called 22-year-old Harmanpreet Singh “a dog”, and physically assaulted him, leaving him with a broken nose in February in Corio. Or when they called 26-year-old Nayonika a “curry muncher”, “smelly Indian”, and a “Mrs. 7/11 driver” in Sydney’s CBD.

But racism also manifests through misinformation such as caricatures portraying Indians, and other immigrants, as being responsible for the housing crisis.

It co-exists in the digital world where desk warriors feel confident to call Greens Senator Mehreen Faruqi “a filthy Australian hating racist pig”.

It does not stop at that. Racism and bigotry also acts through constant daily acts of micro-aggression; through people staring you …

author: Frenny Jowi
title: Congo in Kenya: Why Xenophobia is a Racist Ideal
content:
Thirty-three-year-old Emmanuel is a freelance hairdresser in Nairobi. He is a refugee from the Democratic Republic of Congo and has lived in Kenya for six years.


The young man is chic, dressed in designer brands, with a gentle demeanour that reflects his customer-care style in the city’s beauty industry. His calm, collected appearance belies a history of strife, struggle, and an ongoing effort to recover from the decades of armed conflict he witnessed as a child in North Kivu.


‘I will never forget the night when rebels attacked our village in North Kivu. I must have been seven years old at that time. Some people were killed, and there was fire burning everywhere around us.’


Emmanuel narrated his story as he swung around in his styling chair in front of a large mirror that is popularly called a ‘station’ in Nairobi’s hairdressing and beauty salons.


I had visited Emmanuel at the salon where he works. Renting business premises in Nairobi is a significant cost for many young business owners, whether citizen or foreigner. In the beauty industry, most professionals can only afford to rent a mirror and a styling chair as a workstation – hence the name ‘station’.


While occasionally glancing at his WhatsApp notifications for customer bookings, Emmanuel continued to share his story with me.


‘The attack happened many years ago. I still remember how my mother stopped to pack her pot of fish stew and cassava leaves and rice. My father asked her to hurry up, leave the food, and run for safety, but she insisted she would not leave her delicious food. As we all escaped in the dim light of the moon, I recall our neighbours’ comments about my mother’s weird sense of what to salvage. She insisted the food would also save us and she would not leave it behind despite the gunfire. Now I find that funny.’


Emmanuel laughed, trying to find humour in a devastating story.


I knew that talking about traumatic childhood experiences from war would be difficult, so I did not press Emmanuel further about the night armed fighters attacked their village, killing many people and setting houses on fire.


The events Emmanuel witnessed as a child in 2000 were part of the Second Congo War, dubbed Africa’s World War. According to

Amnesty International

, the DRC’s current conflict has been ongoing since the 1990s, particularly in the eastern part of the country, which borders South Sudan, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, and Tanzania.


This armed conflict escalated in August 1998 when President Laurent Kabila fell out with the Ugandan and Rwandan allies who had helped him seize power.


Emmanuel narrated how the fighting between the Lendu-Ngiti and the opposing Hema began as communal land disputes involving farmers and pastoralists. Locals believe politicians and those with mining interests took advantage of these seemingly solvable disputes to fuel the ongoing war. He added that their radio broadcasts often mentioned various fighting groups such as the UPDF (Uganda People’s Defence Forces) and the UPC (United Congolese Patriots).


‘In the news, when we heard that Bosco Ntaganda was in court and wanted to defend himself in Kinyarwanda, we were all shocked, because locally, we knew him as one of us. We never thought he was from Rwanda. He lived here for so long, spoke our language, looked like one of us, and was always involved in Congolese affairs,’ Emmanuel said.


Decades of conflict have been fuelled by ethnic tensions, political rivalries, corruption, and fighting for control of valuable natural resources.


Over time, the war drew in nine African nations, making it one of the largest wars in African history. The 2017 Kivu Security Tracker Report by Jason Stearns and Christoph Vogel listed 132 armed fighter groups operating in North and South Kivu alone.


Today, Emmanuel is one of the over 100 million citizens of the DRC affected by incessant wars. The DRC is the fourth most populous country in Africa and the 14th in the world. Despite decades of war and pandemics such as Ebola, its population has continued to grow steadily. 


In 2025,

Human Rights Watch

 reported that the Congolese military and a coalition of armed fighters have continued to attack civilians. The report adds that throughout 2024, the

Rwandan

 army and the M23 armed group indiscriminately shelled displacement camps and other densely populated areas near Goma in eastern Congo.


Emmanuel arrived in Kenya in 2019, just before the COVID-19 pandemic. Earlier, in 2017 …

title: Tormenta Negra 2: “no son políticas de prevención del delito, es racismo”
content:
El gobierno de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires realizó el jueves 24 un nuevo operativo “Tormenta Negra” en 15 barrios populares con violencia policial, detenciones arbitrarias y el retiro de pertenencias y herramientas de trabajo. Jorge Macri “consolida una política que identifica pobreza con inseguridad” e insiste en violentar la vida en los barrios populares y atemorizar a quienes viven en ellos, denunciaron desde el Centro de Estudios Legales y Sociales (CELS). “No existen operativos de este tipo en los otros barrios de la Ciudad” como Palermo, Caballito o Núñez, señalaron.


Compartimos el comunicado del CELS:


Tormenta Negra 2: el gobierno de CABA entiende a los barrios populares como zonas de ocupación


El gobierno de Jorge Macri volvió a desplegar más de 1500 policías y agentes de control en 15 villas y barrios populares de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires. Registramos episodios de violencia policial, detenciones arbitrarias y el retiro de pertenencias y herramientas de trabajo. La CABA consolida una política que identifica pobreza con inseguridad, no con ausencia de derechos.


El jueves 24 de septiembre, el gobierno de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires realizó un nuevo operativo Tormenta Negra en 15 villas y barrios populares. Más de 1500 policías y agentes de control de Espacio Público ingresaron de manera simultánea a los barrios para realizar controles de personas y vehículos, inspeccionar comercios y retirar del espacio público objetos de las personas que viven allí. Es la segunda vez que el gobierno porteño organiza un despliegue de estas características, después del de mayo de este año. Jorge Macri insiste en violentar la vida en los barrios populares y atemorizar a quienes viven en ellos.


Se trata de un modo de entender la ciudad y el derecho a la ciudad con un abordaje racializante y con límites de clase. Es una política que decide qué cuerpos van a ser controlados por la policía, qué familias van a ser desalojadas sin garantías, qué personas deberán demostrar una y otra vez que tienen derecho a quedarse y cuáles tienen que mostrar su documentación en las estaciones de trenes y subtes. La política porteña naturaliza que la principal y primera intervención del Estado en los barrios populares va a ser la policial. Uno de los jóvenes detenidos estaba en situación de calle dentro de la Villa 21. El gobierno llegó con patrulleros, efectivos armados y agentes de control, en lugar de organizar una intervención a partir de las necesidades de quienes viven allí o para garantizar los derechos sobre los que el mismo Estado está en deuda. No hubo presencia de áreas de desarrollo social, sino el despliegue de dispositivos de estigmatización de quienes viven allí, para convertirlos en sujetos de sospecha. El gobierno de la Ciudad abandonó las políticas de integración sociourbana. Ahora se enfoca en una política que niega la ciudadanía de las personas que viven en estos barrios. No existen operativos de este tipo en los otros barrios de la Ciudad, que los invadan a la pesca de ver qué delitos se identifican, que sin duda los hay en Palermo, Caballito o Núñez.


La vara en la Ciudad de Buenos Aires está tan baja que tenemos que reiterar lo obvio: en los barrios populares viven personas que trabajan, estudian, crían a sus hijos que van a la escuela y sostienen redes comunitarias. Tienen derecho a tener políticas que integren las villas con la ciudad en términos de derechos garantizados: a la vivienda, a la salud, a la educación, al trabajo y no estar sujeto a control poblacional permanente. La guerra contra los pobres habla de la pobreza en políticas públicas de la gestión actual de la ciudad. Y del solapamiento de un abordaje que se anuncia como control de actividades delictivas con la persecución de las estrategias de supervivencia. De este modo, la ciudad se fragmenta cada vez más. Los operativos espasmódicos y violentos no llevan orden a estos barrios, sino incertidumbre, abusos y show para las redes sociales. Cuando terminan los operativos y la policía se retira de estos barrios, no permanecen otras políticas públicas.


Durante el operativo del jueves registramos situaciones de violencia policial, uso de gases lacrimógenos y disparos de balas de goma. En la Villa 21-24, los registros audiovisuales que hicieron los mismos vecinos muestran intervenciones contra personas en situación de calle que intentaban resguardar sus colchones y pertenencias. title: Programme d'urgence féministe : 13 mesures contre les violences sexistes et sexuelles
content:
Programme d'Urgence Féministe : treize mesures contre les violences sexistes et sexuelles

 

!


Ce programme n'est qu'une étape pour faire reculer les violences. Les éradiquer totalement ne pourra passer que par le renversement complet du système raciste, patriarcal et capitaliste : par la révolution

 

!


Appropriez-vous ce programme, n'hésitez pas à le diffuser, l'imprimer

 

; tract 4 pages en pièce jointe.


 Article d'origine sur

feministesrevolutionnaires.org


Pour qu'il n'y ait plus aucune violence


Depuis l'irruption de #MeToo en 2017, la question des violences sexistes et sexuelles s'est inscrite durablement parmi les préoccupations majeures de la population. Chaque année, le décompte des féminicides fait la une des journaux. Les dénonciations de violences mettant en cause des figures publiques sont largement médiatisées. Les affaires suscitant l'émotion populaire se succèdent.


En parallèle, on observe un développement rapide des mobilisations féministes, avec des marches massives aux dates emblématiques du 8 mars (journée internationale pour les droits des femmes) et du 25 novembre (journée internationale contre les violences de genre). Bien que ses détracteurs restent très audibles, le mouvement féministe gagne en force et en audience et ses idées et ses discours se diffusent amplement.


Malgré ces éléments favorables,

le mouvement féministe peine à faire émerger des revendications concrètes

 capables d'enrayer à grande échelle les violences sexistes et sexuelles. Pourtant, on ne manque pas de ressources pour comprendre les mécanismes qui permettent les violences. Comment expliquer, alors, que nous ayons tant de mal à y répondre

 

?


Il faut dire que

la tâche est d'une ampleur colossale

 : on estime que près de 280 000 femmes et 160 000 enfants sont victimes de violences chaque année. Et le mouvement féministe se fixe comme objectif, ambitieux, de

réduire ces chiffres à zéro

 

! Or les violences sexistes et sexuelles, au-delà des rapports de pouvoir individuels entre un agresseur et sa victime, contribuent à maintenir l'exploitation des femmes. Par la peur, ces violences disciplinent les femmes et les contraignent à des rôles bien précis dans le système capitaliste : effectuer gratuitement les tâches domestiques au sein de leur foyer, subir des emplois sous-payés dans les secteurs les plus dévalorisés du marché du travail (soin, éducation, entretien…). Pour nous, réduire à zéro les violences sexistes et sexuelles, cela nécessite donc de

transformer radicalement la société en détruisant tout le système patriarcal, raciste et capitaliste : de faire la révolution

.


D'ici là, une série d'étapes intermédiaires peuvent faire baisser les violences. Nous avons tenté de les regrouper dans ce


Programme d'urgence féministe en 13 mesures


. En partant d'une analyse sur les causes des violences, nous déterminons quels leviers il faudrait actionner en priorité pour les faire reculer, et, de là, quelles mesures revendiquer.


La précarité : un accélérateur des violences


Si les violences sexistes et sexuelles existent dans toutes les couches de la société, elles ne touchent pas tout le monde de la même manière. On dit souvent que le viol et l'inceste n'ont ni classe sociale, ni couleur de peau, ni religion. Mais en ce qui concerne les violences conjugales et, dans leur forme la plus extrême, le féminicide, certaines conditions sociales augmentent le risque d'y être exposée.


Les données disponibles suggèrent que

la précarité

,

la dépendance économique

 vis-à-vis d'un conjoint et les inégalités de revenus au sein des couples sont des facteurs qui augmentent significativement le risque d'être victime de violences. Ainsi, dans plus de 80% des cas de féminicides conjugaux en France, les victimes sont soit sans emploi ou retraitées, soit ouvrières ou employées

 [

1

]

]. Les cadres et professions intellectuelles supérieures sont, à l'inverse, très peu représentées. Il existe aussi des corrélations entre les pertes d'emploi, les baisses de revenus et l'augmentation des violences dans les foyers

 [

2

]

].


La conclusion est simple :

la dépendance économique à un conjoint violent est un véritable obstacle à la séparation

, d'autant plus avec des enfants à charge et des aides sociales insuffisantes. Par ailleurs, le motif de la séparation non acceptée est le deuxième mobile invoqué par les hommes qui tuent leur compagne.


La précarité n'est pas qu'une question de catégorie …

author: By Camilla Donzelli, Contributor
title: A Failed Reception System in Crete Turns People on the Move Into Political Targets
content:
Athanatoi, Greece — Residents of a small village in Northern Crete, near Herakleion, are fighting the Greek government’s plan to convert a disused factory into a reception center for people on the move, escalating a monthslong standoff that pits xenophobic backlash against an increasingly securitized European border regime. 


“We’re not staying silent. We’re not backing down. No to the camp.” The slogan, painted in red and black across a large banner, hangs from the gate of a factory facing the Candia-Mires state highway, near the village of Athanatoi in northern Crete. A few yards away, a second banner reads: “No camp — the people have a voice.”


A banner reading “We’re not staying silent. We’re not backing down. No to the camp,” hanging from the gate of a factory opposite the abandoned Skouloudis industrial complex. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


Across the road stands the disused Skouloudis industrial complex, recently identified by Greece’s Ministry of Migration and Asylum as a site to be converted into a reception center for migrants crossing the stretch of sea between Libya and Greece and landing on the island’s southern coast. Since Minister Thanos Plevris

announced

 the plan in mid-June 2026, Skouloudis has been at the center of a

bitter standoff

 between authorities and local communities.


The former Skouloudis industrial facility, seen from the Heraklion–Mires state highway. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


The choice of this industrial site, however, is only the latest development in a long and contested decision-making process that began in the summer of 2025, when

arrivals in Crete

 far outpaced those recorded along the Aegean route — the sea passage from Turkey to the Greek islands of Lesbos, Samos and Chios that has long been the country’s primary migration corridor — making the island Greece’s main point of entry.


Against a backdrop of chronic absence of adequate first-reception facilities on the island, the handling of landings has fallen to entirely

unsustainable emergency measures

.


The main temporary holding site in Heraklion remains the former psygeio — a Coast Guard cold-storage building in the port area. Meant to hold just 70 to 80 people, the site held more than 450 in the first months of 2026, forcing men, women and children to sleep on the floor.


The lack of adequate sanitation and ventilation created dire health conditions, while pressure to find an alternative mounted further as the Port Authority pursued legal action to clear the site. Faced with this infrastructural collapse, authorities found themselves forced to publicly propose a solution.


One of the rooms inside the temporary first-reception facility known as Psygeio, in the port of Heraklion, where people are held after their arrival. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


Locked Up and Criminalized: People on the Move Face a Broken System on Crete’s Shores


Between Delay and Denial 


In the summer of 2025, the government

announced

 the conversion of several military sites, but that announcement was followed by months of silence and effective inaction. Only in February 2026 did the Greek Parliament approve the opening of

two centers

, without specifying their location or how they would be built.


The first details came only months later: in Chania, authorities settled on retrofitting

Agya

, a former exhibition center already in use as a temporary reception facility; in Heraklion, the disused Skouloudis industrial plant was identified instead.


“These delays and constant changes of plan shouldn’t be read as political strategy, but as failure,” Michalis Markodimitrakis, a member of the Heraklion-based collective Thalassa of Solidarity and a researcher at the Hellenic Mediterranean University, told Unicorn Riot.


“Local communities and representatives of Crete’s tourism and cultural sector are pushing back hard, because they see the presence of migrants as damaging to the island’s image and a threat to their economic interests.”


Michalis Markodimitrakis, member of Thalassa of Solidarity collective


A side view of the former Skouloudis industrial facility, where adaptation works to accommodate people on the move have not yet begun. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


Back in July 2025, the day after the first announcement floated the opening of the centers, a network of tourism industry associations sent an

open letter

 to Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and Migration and …

author: Thomas Kennedy
title: Florida City That Willingly Signed Deal With ICE Finds Itself in Crisis
content:
Half the population of Doral, Florida, is from Venezuela. Why haven’t its leaders rescinded their deal with ICE?

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

The City of Doral is in crisis. Since Donald Trump returned to office in 2025, the Florida municipality has found itself in the crosshairs of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), with ongoing raids and targeted operations that seem to be intensifying in recent weeks.

Nearly half of Doral’s population is from Venezuela, the largest population of Venezuelans in any city in the United States. This is a diaspora that finds itself under constant attack by the Trump administration, as more than 615,000 have lost or are facing the termination of their temporary protected status (TPS) following revocations, and Venezuelans make up 59 percent of all immigrants affected by mass terminations of TPS designations. These are the same people who now find themselves in the crosshairs of enforcement operations in Doral. The recent earthquakes in Caracas that have killed thousands and destroyed critical infrastructure did nothing to stop these attacks against Venezuelan immigrants, despite the country obviously being in no condition to receive hundreds of thousands of these nationals back if they were to be deported.

Despite presiding over such a vulnerable population, Doral’s government was one of the first in the state to sign a 287(g) agreement under the second Trump administration, deputizing local police with specific federal immigration enforcement powers. The mayor and council members did this under no requirement, mandate, or obligation, as Florida statute requires only counties and sheriff’s departments operating jails or detention facilities to sign these types of agreements, and Doral operates neither.

Doral’s government was one of the first in the state to sign a 287(g) agreement deputizing local police with specific federal immigration enforcement powers.

Now that public sentiment is turning against them, amid the draconian immigration enforcement we see across the country daily, Doral politicians are trying to have it both ways. Mayor Christi Fraga continues to mischaracterize the 287(g) agreement that the city signed under her tenure, falsely claiming that it is not a direct partnership with ICE, and that the state of Florida obligated Doral to sign on. As already established, this is simply not true, and Fraga claims that the city can’t rescind the agreement because their “responsibility as elected officials is to follow the law as it exists.” Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier has claimed that cities like Doral can’t revoke 287(g) agreements because this would create a de facto sanctuary city jurisdiction. This is nonsense, as Doral still falls under the correctional jurisdiction of Miami-Dade County, which actively funnels people from its local jails into ICE detention.

It seems Fraga, who supported the signing of the 287(g) contract in Doral, may be obfuscating in this manner because she doesn’t want to burn any political capital rescinding the agreement and would rather do photo ops with Trump. During the president’s visit to Doral for the “Shield of the Americas” Summit, Fraga sat next to him during a meal, even as heightened levels of immigration enforcement under his administration are separating her constituents’ families. When asked for comment for this article Fraga responded by sharing a letter she sent to Florida’s Attorney General James Uthmeier asking for legal clarification on whether localities are obligated to remain in the 287(g) program, which Uthmeier has not responded to.

Similarly, Doral Councilman Rafael Pineyro, who voted in favor of Doral’s 287(g) agreement, is trying to have it both ways as a Republican who supported Trump and has not outright broken with him, but who is increasingly pushing back as hardline immigration crackdowns intensify in Doral.

Pushing back with mumbled statements and an ineffectual letter expressing disagreement with the rescinding of TPS and stating that the “law can be enforced without losing our humanity,” Pineyro exemplifies the do-nothing approach of politicians across South Florida who supported Trump, who in turn paid them back by separating families and creating chaos in our neighborhoods. Pineyro did not respond by press time when offered the chance to comment.

author: free_demos
title: The Revolutionary Legacy of the Balkans: Yavor Tarinski’s Balkan Federation and Communes
content:
A forgotten history of Balkan federalism, communes and internationalist struggle


By Giorgos Chatzinakos, human geographer, researcher and writer on the commons, self-government and emancipatory politics


Author


Giorgos Chatzinakos


    Submitted by

free_demos

 on October 2, 2026


The social and political history of the Balkans


The socio-political history of the peoples of the Balkans has always been multifaceted and interconnected: a complex world shaped by affinities as much as by contradictions. During the nineteenth century, the ideas of the French Revolution travelled like seeds of freedom on the winds of history, searching for fertile ground across the already turbulent Balkan Peninsula.


The Balkans were never a timeless landscape of harmony, but they were a deeply plural space in which linguistic, religious and cultural communities had lived beside one another for centuries. As Ottoman rule receded, the intervention of the Great Powers and the advance of competing imperial and national projects transformed that world. The nation-state offered a powerful language of emancipation, but it also hardened borders, rival territorial claims and exclusive national histories. The result was not simply liberation from empire, but new hierarchies, new antagonisms and, at times, the violent purification of populations in the name of the nation.


This is the history through which the Balkans are still too often imagined: nationalism, violence, ethnic antagonism and fragmentation. The very word “Balkanisation” entered political language as a synonym for disintegration. Yet this familiar narrative obscures another political inheritance, one that was equally present in the struggles of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.


Against this teleology of inevitable nation-states stands what Andrej Grubačić, in

Don’t Mourn, Balkanize!

[1], calls “the persistent vision of a surprisingly consistent utopia”. The Paris Commune of 1871 became one of the great reference points for this political imagination. Its fire reappeared in the Bosnian uprising of 1875 and survived the geopolitical settlement imposed by the Treaty of Berlin in 1878. In 1903, the Ilinden–Preobrazhenie Uprising, the short-lived Kruševo Republic and the Strandzha Commune offered further glimpses of a different Balkan future: not a landscape ordered only by kings, governments and armies, but one of peoples, communes and federations struggling to organise life from below.


Figure 1. Group of revolutionaries with a red flag in Kruševo, July 1903. The horseman in fustanella at the far left is the local commander Pitu Guli, a leading figure in the Macedonian-Adrianople revolutionary movement. A few  days later, he fell fighting the Ottoman army on the outskirts of the town.


Yavor Tarinski’s

Balkan Federation and Communes: Revolutionary Projects in Bulgaria of the 19th & 20th Centuries

[2] returns to this buried revolutionary inheritance. First published in Greek by Aftoleksi in 2023[3] and now being published in English by PM Press, the book examines revolutionary projects in nineteenth- and early twentieth-century Bulgaria that cultivated the ideas of the Balkan Federation and the commune. Tarinski’s central intervention is historiographical as much as political: he asks what becomes visible when Balkan history is read not from the standpoint of victorious states, but from the defeated possibilities of autonomy, federation and social revolution.


A history from below, against nationalist memory


This is where the book is at its strongest. It does not simply add several forgotten episodes to an established national story; it unsettles the story itself. In a region where historical memory remains heavily organised through the nation-state, recovering suppressed traditions of cooperation and self-government becomes a way of reopening the political imagination. An unrealised past was once a possible future.


Tarinski’s genealogy reaches further back than the nineteenth-century revolutionary movements. He points to earlier communal forms and dissident traditions, including Slavic assemblies, the Bogomils and the Commune of Zealots in fourteenth-century Thessaloniki. These episodes are very different from one another and should not be collapsed into a single continuous lineage. Their significance in the book is rather to challenge the assumption that centralised statehood is the natural or only political grammar of Balkan history.

author: Regine Nguini
title: African Newsrooms Can No Longer Delay Creating the Conditions for Women to Stay
content:
When one Black South African journalist decided to leave the profession after only four years, she did not walk away because she had stopped believing in journalism: ‘I mourned because I knew I could have done so much in that space.’


Her experience is documented in a

2025 Reuters Institute fellowship paper by South African journalist Bongekile Macupe

. After difficult experiences in the newsroom, including during her pregnancy, the journalist eventually decided to leave. Yet her words suggest that what disappeared with her departure was not her passion for journalism, but the possibility of what she might have contributed had the conditions allowed her to stay.


That sense of loss is part of what the

Kigali Declaration on the Elimination of Gender Violence in and through Media in Africa by 2034

 is trying to prevent.


Led by African Women in Media (AWiM), the Declaration calls for action across the media ecosystem; from media organisations and professional associations to journalists, journalism educators, funders, digital platforms and regulators, to address gender violence both within media institutions and through the content they produce.


Its ambition builds on a problem that has been documented for years: for many women journalists across Africa, entering a newsroom is only the first step. Staying, progressing and practising journalism without discrimination, harassment or violence can prove to be another challenge altogether.


Entering journalism is not enough


In 2020, AWiM and Fojo Media Institute published

Barriers to Women Journalists in Sub-Saharan Africa

 based on questionnaire responses from 125 women journalists across 17 African countries, alongside interviews and focus groups. Significantly, the research did not look only at women’s ability to enter journalism. It examined barriers to entering, progressing and

staying in the profession.


The women who participated had entered journalism with strong ambitions. Passion, societal good and the desire to tell overlooked stories emerged prominently among their motivations.


One Kenyan journalist explained: ‘I loved the career and still do because I wanted to inform and highlight some issues affecting people in remote communities.’


Another participant described journalism as a way of telling ‘untold stories’ capable of influencing policy and improving people’s lives. Yet the professional environments encountered by women did not always nurture those ambitions.


The AWiM study identified job stagnation and salary disparities, gendered allocation of assignments, sexual harassment, bullying, sexism and racial discrimination, family responsibilities and unequal access to leadership among the barriers affecting women’s careers.


The research also documented how gendered expectations around family life could affect retention. Women spoke about the difficulty of reconciling journalism with childcare and family responsibilities, particularly when combined with poor pay and limited opportunities for progression.


The contrast is striking: women described entering journalism because they wanted to tell stories, serve communities and create change, while the structures of the profession could eventually make remaining within it difficult.


The question, therefore, is not simply whether women can become journalists. It is whether the conditions exist for them to remain journalists.


When leaving becomes an option


Macupe’s 2025 Reuters Institute paper brings that question into sharper focus. She interviewed ten Black African women with newsroom experience ranging from one year to more than 30 years in South Africa. One of the observations that troubled her most was generational: younger journalists described experiences echoing those of women who had entered the profession decades earlier.


The women spoke about unequal access to opportunities and resources, exclusion from networks of influence and repeated challenges to their authority. One former journalist described the informal networks she saw operating around her: ‘These guys are all friends. They drink together. They party together… if a position comes up, the first person they think of is another guy. It can never be a woman.’


Another woman described the daily struggle of managing men who resisted her authority: ‘You have to assert your authority all the time. And it becomes a daily struggle. Every day you are fighting.’


For some, eventually, leaving became preferable to continuing …

author: daniel
title: hätte, hätte, menschenwürde
content:
Mit El Hishri ist ein ganzes System der Gewalt angeklagt

Das Komitee für Grundrechte und Demokratie ringt seit mittlerweile 46 Jahren mit den vielfältigen Fragen rund um Menschenrechte, radikale Demokratie und Menschenwürde – und wie diese von unten immerzu neu erkämpft werden müssen. In der Kolumne „Hätte, hätte, Menschenwürde“ schreiben die Komiteeler*innen ab sofort in jeder Ausgabe über aktuelle Ereignisse und Auseinandersetzungen, die sie umtreiben.

Am 16. Juli 2025 vollstreckten deutsche Behörden einen Strafbefehl des Internationalen Strafgerichtshofs (IStGH). Der Libyer Mohamed Ali El Hishri wurde am Flughafen Berlin-Brandenburg von der Bundespolizei verhaftet. Der Prozess soll am 4. Mai 2027 beginnen. Der IStGH verfolgt Einzelpersonen für Völkermord, Verbrechen gegen die Menschlichkeit und Kriegsverbrechen, wenn der Staat des Tatorts oder des Täters nicht willens oder fähig ist, zu ermitteln. Die Vollstreckung von Haftbefehlen des IStGH durch Deutschland ist keineswegs selbstverständlich: Friedrich Merz hatte bezüglich des Haftbefehls gegen den israelischen Ministerpräsidenten Netanjahu angekündigt, im Falle eines geplanten Deutschlandbesuchs dessen Ein- und Ausreise ohne Festnahme zu ermöglichen. Im Falle El Hishri ist die Anerkennung des IStGH für die Bundesregierung jedoch opportun.

Laut Anklage des IStGH soll Khaled Mohamed Ali El Hishri als hochrangiger Funktionär der bewaffneten Gruppe Spezialeinsatzkräfte (SDF/RADA) zuständig für den Bereich des Gefängnisses Mitiga in Libyschen Tripoli gewesen sein. Das Gefängnis in Mitiga zählt zu den staatlich anerkannten Gefängnissen, obwohl es faktisch von einer bewaffneten Miliz betrieben wird. Dort sind Frauen und Kinder inhaftiert. El Hishri werden Verbrechen an Gefangenen vorgeworfen, unter ihnen libysche Staatsangehörige sowie Migrant- *innen und Geflüchtete. Die Anklage umfasst Folter und andere unmenschliche Handlungen, Vergewaltigung und andere Formen sexualisierter Gewalt, Mord, versuchten Mord und Versklavung. Im Dezember 2025 wurde El Hishri nach Den Haag überstellt.

Insbesondere Schwarze Menschen aus den Ländern Afrikas werden in Libyen versklavt und sind systematischer Ausbeutung und Misshandlung ausgesetzt. Durch Erpressung, Zwangsarbeit, Lösegeldforderungen und Menschenhandel werden sie zur Ware degradiert. Das Geschäft mit Flüchtenden ist ein äußerst profitabler Wirtschaftszweig, das Mitiga-Gefängnis ist Teil davon. Mit offizieller Anerkennung können Gefängnisse zudem Hilfsgüter und Gelder von Organisationen wie IOM (Internationale Organisation für Migration) beziehen. Sie sind Teil eines Systems gewaltvoller Rückführungen (Pull- bzw. Pushbacks), das die EU-Mitgliedstaaten mittels Institutionen wie der Europäischen Grenzschutzagentur Frontex und Milizen der sogenannten Libyschen Küstenwache erschaffen haben, um die Migration nach Europa zu minimieren. Die EU-Staaten, darunter Deutschland, finanzieren, unterstützen und trainieren die sogenannte libysche Küstenwache, die Überwachungsflugzeuge von Frontex informieren diese über Boote, die sich von Libyen aus über das Mittelmeer in Richtung Europa bewegen. Auf diese Weise werden Flüchtende aufgegriffen und zurück nach Libyen in eben dieses Gewaltsystem gezwungen, von dem das Mitiga-Gefängnis ein brutaler Baustein ist.

Bislang haben sich bereits 120 Überlebende des Mitiga-Gefängnisses beim IStGH gemeldet, um Zeugnis abzulegen über das, was sie unter El Hishri in Libyen haben erleben müssen. Für viele von ihnen bietet eine Anhörung in Den Haag die erste Gelegenheit, das Erlebte offiziell zu schildern. Für sie alle ist es außerdem von entscheidender Bedeutung, dass in dem Prozess nicht allein El Hishri anklagt wird. Die Überlebenden wollen, dass deutlich wird, wie die EU-Politik zu der Gewalt beiträgt, der sie in Libyen ausgesetzt waren, nachdem sie durch die libyschen Milizen auf dem Meer aufgegriffen, zurückgeschafft und inhaftiert wurden. Sie fordern, dass die Verantwortung der Europäischen Staaten ermittelt wird.

Folter und Misshandlung dauern an

Während El Hishri Verbrechen aus den Jahren 2014 bis 2020 vorgeworfen werden, gehen Folter und Misshandlungen in Mitiga und anderen staatlichen und in den nicht-offiziellen Gefängnissen Libyens bis heute weiter. Wir müssen zur Kenntnis nehmen, dass diese Gefängnisse faktisch längst das tun, was die EU-Staaten mit GEAS und den Return Hubs planen: das Festsetzen von Migrant*innen im Vorfeld der EU-Außengrenzen mit beschränktem bis keinem Zugang zu …

title: Almanya: Türkiyeli göçmen ailenin oğlu Belit Onay ikinci kez Hanover'in başında
content:
Almanya'nın Aşağı Saksonya eyaletinin başkenti Hannover'de seçmenler, Türkiye'den göçmeni bir işçi ailesinin oğlu olan Yeşiller Partisi adayı Belit Onay'ı ikinci kez belediye başkanlığına getirdi.


27 Eylül'de yapılan ikinci turda sandıkların tamamının sayılarak sonucun açıklanmasıyla Onay'ın, oyların yüzde 61,5'ini; rakibi Sosyal Demokrat Partili (SPD) Axel von der Ohe'nin ise  yüzde 38,5'ini aldığı kesinleşti. Seçime katılım oranı yüzde 45 oldu. Yaklaşık 397 bin kayıtlı seçmenin bulunduğu kentte Onay böylece 2019'da başladığı belediye başkanlığı görevini bir dönem daha sürdürecek.


Başarının kaynağı dar topluluk dayanışmasının ötesinde 


Sonucun Almanya'nın göç ve çok kültürlülük tartışmaları açısından taşıdığı anlam, yalnızca Türkiye kökenli bir siyasetçinin ülkenin büyük kentlerinden birinin başında kalmasından kaynaklanmıyor. Onay'ın aldığı oy büyüklüğü, başarının bir etnik topluluğun kendi adayının arkasında birleşmesiyle açıklanmasını da tartışma dışı bırakıyor.


Hannover Belediyesi verilerine göre, 558 bin 767 nüfuslu kentin nüfusunun yüzde 23'ünü yabancı ülke vatandaşları oluşturuyor. Alman vatandaşlığına sahip göçmenler ve göçmen ailelerin çocukları da hesaba katıldığında “ailevi göç geçmişi" sahibi nüfusun oranı yüzde 44'e çıkıyor. Başka bir ifadeyle, göç artık Hannover'de küçük bir azınlığın özelliği değil, kentin demografik yapısının temel unsurlarından biri⁠


Dahası, 2015'ten bu yana Almanya'ya göç ederek Hannover'e yerleşenler tek başına kent nüfusunun yüzde 12,4'ünü oluşturuyor. Bunların yarısından fazlası 2022'den sonra geldi. Dolayısıyla Onay'ın yönettiği Hannover, Almanya'nın son on yıldaki göç dalgalarının kent toplumunu nasıl değiştirdiğine dair somut örneklerden biri. 


İkinci turda desteğini büyüttü


Onay'ın sonucu ikinci tur aritmetiği açısından da dikkat çekici.


13 Eylül'deki ilk turda dokuz aday yarışmış; Onay yüzde 45,6 ile açık ara birinci olmuştu. SPD'li von der Ohe yüzde 21,5, CDU adayı Peter Karst yüzde 14,1, AfD adayı Jessica Miriam Schülke ise yüzde 10,8 almıştı. Hiçbir aday mutlak çoğunluğa ulaşamadığı için Onay ile von der Ohe ikinci tura kaldı


İkinci turda Onay'ın desteği yüde 61,5'e yükseldi. Bu sonuç, yalnızca Yeşiller seçmeninin değil, ilk turda elenen adaylara oy veren seçmenlerin de önemli bir bölümünün görevdeki belediye başkanına yöneldiğini gösteriyor. Ancak ayrıntılı seçmen geçiş verileri henüz yayımlanmadı. Bu aşamada hangi parti seçmeninin hangi oranda Onay'a geçtiğini kesin olarak söylemek söz konusu değil. 


Onay seçimden sonra aldığı geniş desteğe işaret ederek “Bu kadar büyük bir desteğin bulunmasından memnunum” dedi ve ikinci döneminde de “bu kentteki bütün insanların belediye başkanı” olacağını söyledi.


Yeni dönemde Hannover'i daha dayanışmacı ve iklim dostu hale getirmeyi ve kentte toplumsal bütünlüğü güçlendirmeyi amaçladığını belirten Onay, belediye meclisindeki demokratik partilere de birlikte çalışma çağrısı yaptı.


Bir göçmen işçi ailesinden belediye başkanlığına


15 Ocak 1981'de Aşağı Saksonya'nın Goslar kentinde Türkiye'den Almanya'ya "misafir işçi" statüsüyle gelmiş bir işçi ailesinin çocuğu olarak doğan Belit Onay, Hannover'de hukuk öğrenimi gördü. 2011'de Hannover Belediye Meclisi'ne, 2013'te Yeşiller adına Aşağı Saksonya Eyalet Meclisi'ne girdi ve 2019'a kadar milletvekilliği yaptı. Aynı yıl Hannover Büyükşehir Belediye Başkanlığına seçildi.⁠


Yedi yıl sonra seçmenin önüne artık göçmen kökenli bir “ilk” olarak değil, icraatlarıyla değerlendirilen bir belediye başkanı olarak çıktı. Onay'ın aile geçmişi hep aynı kalırken oyunun durmadan artarak yüzde 61,5'e varması siyasal desteğinin kökeninin çok ötesine yayıldığını ortaya koydu.


Hannover'de çocukların çoğunun kökeninde göç geçmişi var


Hannover'in nüfus yapısı da Almanya'da “göçmen” ve “yerli” kategorilerinin, özellikle büyük kentlerde, giderek birbirlerinden daha zor ayırt edilebilen iki topluluğu tanımladığını gösteriyor.


Kentte ailevi göç geçmişi olan nüfus 2021 sonunda yaklaşık 215 bin iken, 2025 sonunda 246 bine çıktı. Bu, nüfusun tamamının yüzde 44'ünü oluşturuyor. Aynı oran 18 yaş altındaki çocuk ve gençlerde yüzde 63,2'. Başka bir deyişle, Hannover'in yeni kuşağında göç geçmişi olanlar artık açık farkla çoğunluğu oluşturuyorlar.


Üstelik bu nüfus tek bir etnik kökene bağlı bir “göçmen topluluğu” oluşturmuyor. Kentte Türkiye, Ukrayna ve Suriye başta olmak üzere çok farklı kökenlerden gelen topluluklar var; son yıllardaki göçün önemli bir bölümününün kaynağında da çalışma …
