author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: "No Land to Stand On": Mahmoud Khalil on His Memoir, Palestine, Fighting Deportation & Suing Columbia
content:
We speak with Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil about his new memoir,

No Land to Stand On: Notes from Detention

. It details his 104 days of detention inside a Louisiana

ICE

 jail after he was targeted for arrest and deportation by the Trump administration over his pro-Palestine campus advocacy at Columbia University. Khalil missed the birth of his first child, Deen, while he was separated from his wife, Noor Abdalla, who is a U.S. citizen. The administration is still trying to deport Khalil, who has launched civil rights lawsuits against the government and Columbia University over his treatment.


“Eighteen months after my arrest, this administration has never charged me with any crime or even presented any evidence that I committed any crimes, yet they are able to get away with this because I’m Palestinian,” Mahmoud tells

Democracy Now!


Khalil’s memoir also looks beyond his own case, recounting the people he met behind bars and what their stories taught him about the broader human cost of the U.S. immigration detention system. “This book is about a story of so many incredible men, fathers and workers who came here seeking safety and a better future, only to be snatched off the street,” he says.

author: Michael_1973
title: On Che Guevara Road: Refugees on the frontlines against fascism
content:
South Africa has a long history of xenophobic violence. The pogroms of 2008 and 2015 are the best known, but over the last two years xenophobic has taken a more organised and more openly political form. It is now a very well organised fascist project, acting with state support and complicity.

March and March was formed in Durban in early 2025 under the leadership of Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma. It presented itself as a citizens’ organisation that only wanted the migration law enforced. In practice it made no distinction between documented and undocumented people. With the uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP), ActionSA and others, it led marches that included armed men while the police stood down.

A ‘deadline’ was announced for migrants to leave the country by 30 June 2026. As that date came closer, local groups went from neighbourhood to neighbourhood threatening and assaulting people and driving them from their homes. Many had their homes, property and businesses seized. Thousands were displaced.

On 18 May 2026 hundreds of refugees who had been driven from their homes went to Refugee Social Services and then to Durban Central Police Station to ask for protection. The police attacked them after which they fled to a church building where supporters of March and March and the Jacob Zuma's uMkhonto weSizwe Party tried to attack them. The state’s answer was to ‘verify’ their papers. Around 400 people taken to the Refugee Reception Centre on Che Guevara Road, where all but two were found to have valid documents. From 22 May to 15 September 2026 they lived on Che Guevara Road, where two died.

Το διήμερο που οργανώνουμε στις 3 και 4 Οκτώβρη 2026 στο δέντρο μνήμης στην παραλία, είναι αφιερωμένο στην «τύχη» των ατόμων που επέζησαν, στην κρατική αντιμετώπιση της ομάδας Anubis με τους ειδικά εκπαιδευμένους σκύλους έρευνας, στη δράση της ομάδας Μέχρι τέλους, στην αποτίμηση του κινήματος για τα Τέμπη, στο θέμα της γενικότερης ασφάλειας στις συγκοινωνίες. Κάθε συμβολή στον προβληματισμό μας είναι πολύτιμη.


Η στήριξη του αγώνα όσων η ζωή ανατράπηκε στα Τέμπη είναι υπόθεση όλων μας. Ο μόνος τρόπος για να υπάρξει δικαίωση είναι η ανάπτυξη μιας κοινωνικής δυναμικής που θα αγωνιστεί γι’ αυτήν.

Rendez-vous mercredi 7 octobre à partir de 18 h 30, aux Clameurs, à Lyon.

author: Branko Marcetic
title: According to Polls, Americans Like Socialism a Lot
content:
A crop of recent polls shows that socialism’s appeal is surprisingly broad. They also reflect a transformed US political landscape that is ripe for a socialist politician to capitalize on — if they’re willing to step up.

Socialism is more popular than it’s been for a long time, both socialism and its most well-known adherents appeal to a surprisingly diverse voter base, and most people still have no idea who Hasan Piker is.

Those are just a few of the takeaways from a crop of polls conducted over the past month or so, which together suggest the radicalized, antiestablishment zeal that’s taken over the Democratic electorate and opened the door for a rising socialist insurgency is still going strong, with a few surprises in tow. And they come at a potentially crucial time, as socialist Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez weighs whether to make a run for president in 2028, a campaign that many socialists view as pivotal to the future prospects of their movement as a whole.

We should obviously be careful with polls, which are not actual elections and only give us an imperfect snapshot of public opinion at any point in time. Still, while they may not exactly reflect hard numbers, they do often reflect real trends, especially when put alongside other poll results. And as such, these recent ones offer several takeaways.

A new Gallup poll conducted over the month of August puts socialism at its highest positive rating, 43 percent, since the polling firm started asking Americans in 2010. Socialism has hovered just under the 40 point mark every year since, until experiencing a pronounced uptick since last year.

Maybe more significant is the reason for this uptick, which according to Gallup isn’t to do with the attitudes of Democrats — their roughly two-thirds positive view has effectively stayed flat since last year — but thanks to independents, whose positive views of socialism have gone 8 points up to 45 percent.

To be clear, socialism still has a way to go. The same Gallup poll found that capitalism is viewed significantly more positively at 55 percent, effectively unchanged from last year, as is “free enterprise” at 77 percent — which, somewhat confusingly, fell 4 points since last year, part of a more gradual downward slide it’s experienced since 2019. On the other hand, “big business” is in the doldrums, hitting a new low of 35 percent this year.

And socialism’s appeal remains geographically specific. According to a recent New York Times/Siena University poll of likely voters nationwide, socialism’s favorability is underwater in all four regions polled but is strongest in the West (-8), and weakest in the South (-27). In a Times/Siena poll of Michigan specifically later this month, Detroit was the only region where it was close to breaking even (-1).

Nevertheless, though 43 percent isn’t a majority, recent history shows that may not matter. Less than a quarter (24 percent) of Americans viewed the MAGA movement positively in April 2023, a year and a half before Donald Trump and MAGA routed the Democrats and took total control of the federal government. The Gallup results here track with several other recent polls that show voters are significantly more open to voting for a socialist candidate than a MAGA politician.

The general narrative is that socialism is mostly popular with young, well-off, and highly educated white progressives. This recent wave of survey results does continue to show there’s a marked generational divide in socialist support. But other than that, this narrative about socialism being confined to a particular demographic slice isn’t really supported by the data.

In the Gallup poll, socialism has more support from people of color and those earning less than $100,000 than from white adults and those earning more than that figure. And its support is about the same whether someone went to college or not. In fact, other than adults aged thirty-four and younger, people of color are the only group that views socialism more positively than capitalism.

We saw a similar result in the Times/Siena nationwide poll, in which white voters had the least favorable view of socialism (-26), followed by the “other non-white” category (-18), while black and Latino voters viewed it most favorably (+4 for each).

Interestingly, that poll does show an educational divide, but one that breaks down along race: while white voters of any educational level hold a very dim view of socialism (a net negative in the double …

author: ROAPE
title: What is the Real Marxist Tradition in Africa?
content:
John Molyneux’s classic statement of Marxist theory and practice

What is the Real Marxist Tradition

? was first published in 1984. The short book provided an incredibly sophisticated description of Marx’s method, and his relentless and insistent focus on the core agency of the working class.


Only the working class – however it is interpreted, described or labelled in social theory – can deliver a revolutionary anti-capitalist project. There cannot be, Molyneux argued, any substitute – no enlightened project of state development, or ‘socialist’ military leadership who deliver socialism on behalf of working people. Molyneux – in restating Marx’s central tenet – emphasised the role of the working class in their self-emancipation. Marx was the original prophet of the self-emancipation by working people. Without this class, and this project, there is simply no Marxism, no socialism, and no possibility of international revolution.


For an African audience the book speaks to multiple failed projects of socialism delivered by military coups, ‘enlightened’ governments and guerrilla movements. Each of these movements at different times dressed themselves in the language of Marxism, class and anti-imperialism but systematically broke genuine efforts at working class power.


What is the Real Marxist Tradition

? speaks directly to those on the continent trying to find a way to a genuine and emancipatory theory and practice of liberation.


Molyneux’ brilliant short book has now been reissued by the UK based publisher Bookmarks, and the Ugandan publisher Editor House Facility (EHF) who focus on readers across the African continent.


The new issue of the book comes with a major new introduction by the Ghanian socialist Gyekye Tanoh. Tanoh writes about the development and transformation of the working class on the continent since Molyneux wrote the book, and the continued capacity of this class to bring about socialist and revolutionary transformation across Africa.  


Join us for the launch of the African edition of

What is the Real Marxist Tradition?

 on 22 October at 18.30 (BST) with Gyekye Tanoh, Tafadzwa Choto

, 

Martin Empson and Mark Thomas. Reserve your place 

here

.


For readers based in Africa, John Molyneux’s 

What is the Real Marxist Tradition?

 can be purchased through Editor House Facility


here

. 


Endorsements of the book:


‘John Molyneux cuts through a century of distortion to recover Marxism’s authentic, revolutionary essence. This classic work distinguishes between living theory and dead orthodoxy, showing that Marxism is not a relic of the past but a vital method for understanding and transforming the world. It is essential reading for anyone seeking to understand capitalism and how to change it. For young activists and students alike, it is a must-read as it offers a powerful weapon for today’s struggles.’ 


Tafadzwa Choto

, International Socialist Organisation, Zimbabwe


‘In this book, John Molyneux undertakes a principled exercise by applying Marxism as a “method of analysis” to Marxism itself. He thereby provides not just a description of what Marxism is, but a method for detecting what isn’t. His application of this exercise—in the form of an autopsy of the interests and classes represented by three self-proclaimed Marxist tendencies—provides a valuable model for defining Marxist politics and organizations in our own contexts while enabling us to avoid the “hybrid ideologies of the petty bourgeoisie.” This is crucial, for us in the Global South, where reality differs greatly from that of Europe, thereby demanding a Marxism of contextualized design, not rigid imitation. The method offered is therefore a vital tool in enabling Marxist projects capable of fulfilling its role in “guiding revolutions to victory.” Such is true whether in the Global South or in global contexts marked by increasing economic complications and the co-option of Marxism by bourgeois ideologies fighting for survival amid the clear failure of neoliberal models … One need not agree with all of Molyneux’s conclusions to find his method a timely and indispensable resource.’


Muzan Alneel

,Marxist researcher and writer from Sudan

What is the Real Marxist Tradition in Africa?

title: "If Bolsonaro wins, they kill us; if Lula wins, they let us die.” : On the 2026 Elections in Brazil
content:
In Brazil, the third term of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of the Workers’ Party is drawing to a close. Lula could win a fourth term—making him the most-elected politician in the country’s history—if he defeats the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. However, Flávio Bolsonaro—son of the man dubbed the “Trump of the Tropics,” who attempted

a
coup d’état in 2023

 strikingly similar to the one Donald Trump attempted in 2021—is dangerously close to taking the lead in the polls.


It is time to assess the threats that a new Bolsonaro administration would pose, as well as the risks that will remain or emerge under a continuing center-left government. We spoke with fellow Brazilian anarchists active on a variety of fronts about the challenges that both scenarios could pose to human beings, the environment, and social movements resisting capitalism and colonialism.


Flavio Bolsonaro in a photo-op with Trump in May 2026 during a meeting at which he lobbied for the US to designate Brazilian drug cartels as “terrorist groups.”


What the 2026 Elections Mean for Brazil and the Americas


The 2026 election will determine to what extent the gains achieved through hard-fought social struggles are stripped away. Just as Trump returned to power via the 2024 election, there is a risk that Flávio Bolsonaro could resume his father’s attacks on the working class, marginalized groups, women, Indigenous peoples, and the environment. The Workers’ Party and the left in general have not managed to produce new figures to succeed their charismatic leader; without Lula, they appear doomed to electoral defeat.


There is a risk that the left will fail to field an effective new candidate for 2030, when Lula will no longer be eligible for reelection. It is also likely that, if elected, Lula could fall victim to the so-called “

incumbency
crisis

“—a pattern that has emerged in elections worldwide this decade. Leaders on both the left and the right see their public standing erode after taking office, as they fail to address the inexorable impact of capitalism on the lives of ordinary people. Symbolism and abstract ideology carry significant weight in the increasingly polarized political landscapes of bourgeois electoral politics, and around the world, the ruling class is relying less and less on the carrot and more and more on the stick.


Therefore, it is likely that the far right will soon return to power. This is a reality we must face. It could happen in 2030, but it could occur as early as 2026.


This is taking place in a context in which Trump’s United States is attempting to reorganize the world order through force, showing everyone what anarchists have always known: that representative democracy, international law, and institutions like the United Nations exist at the pleasure of the ruling class and will not protect us. In the course of its first fourteen months in power, the second Trump administration toppled two heads of state—killing the Iranian leader and abducting the Venezuelan president. In both cases, there was open talk of seizing the oil from these territories; in Venezuela, the administration successfully stole billions of barrels, which are now under Washington’s control.


As head of state, Flávio Bolsonaro would voluntarily hand over Brazilian workers, forests, and land to US imperial interests. We are already in a dire situation under the neoliberal arrangement that Lula manages; with a fascist who is beholden to the US in power, the struggle for survival would become even harder. Furthermore, the oil, minerals, rivers, and forests in the territory known as Brazil would serve to fuel the technological, military, and nuclear arms race that endangers life across the entire planet.


The United States is openly attempting to interfere in Brazilian elections to favor Bolsonaro by sending “observers” to

question
election results

 and threatening to impose further tariffs on Brazil. At the same time, the US-based company Meta—which controls much of the content circulating on social media—is

blocking
Lula’s campaign content

 just weeks before the election without explanation. The same elites with the same reactionary agenda control both military power and the companies that dominate technology and digital communication.

title: Die Welle der Ultrarechten in Lateinamerika: Das Wirtschaftsprogramm der Libertären ist kein Weg zur Freiheit, sondern zur Entfremdung und Unterdrückung
content:
Dossier


„… In den letzten Jahren sind die Regierungen in mehreren lateinamerikanischen Ländern von einer Welle rechtsgerichteter, liberal-konservativer politischer Akteure übernommen worden. Auf der Grundlage klassischer neoliberaler und konservativer Programme gewannen Nayib Bukele in El Salvador, Daniel Noboa in Ecuador, Jair Bolsonaro in Brasilien und Javier Milei in Argentinien die Präsidentschaftswahlen in ihren Ländern. Obwohl es Bolsonaro 2022 nicht gelang, seine Amtszeit als Präsident zu verlängern, befürworteten rund 50 Prozent der brasilianischen Wähler seine ultrarechte Agenda. Dadurch steht die politische Macht des siegreichen Sozialdemokraten Lula da Silva auf wackeligen Füßen. Im Falle Perus wurde der linksgerichtete Präsident Pedro Castillo durch seine frühere Vizepräsidentin Dina Boluarte ersetzt – mit der Zustimmung und der unmittelbaren Allianz der Ultrarechten im Kongress…“

Beitrag des Redaktionsausschusses Minga

in der Übersetzung von Susanne Schartz-Laux am 22. März 2024 in amerika21


 und mehr daraus/dazu:


Was die extreme Rechte in Lateinamerika so stark macht


„Auf dem lateinamerikanischen Kontinent schreitet eine reaktionäre Welle voran. Mit Ausnahme von Mexiko und Brasilien – den beiden Großmächten der Region – sowie Uruguay und Guatemala haben die übrigen Länder (Argentinien, Chile, Kolumbien, Bolivien, Peru, Ecuador, Paraguay, El Salvador, Honduras, Panama usw.) autoritäre rechtsextreme Regierungen gewählt, auch wenn teilweise in Stichwahlen und mit knapper Mehrheit. Dabei handelt es sich um Regierungen, die eine Bevölkerungsstimmung der Feindseligkeit und der politischen Aggressivität zum Ausdruck bringen. Es ist nicht dieselbe traditionelle liberale oder „republikanische“ Rechte, die den triumphierenden Neoliberalismus der 1980er Jahre prägte. (…) Die extreme Rechte von heute verspricht keine Zukunft des Weltfriedens auf der Grundlage der Märkte, sondern eine apokalyptische Säuberung von den Gottlosen, die sich den „natürlichen“ Hierarchien widersetzen: Arbeitgeber:innen über Arbeitnehmer:innen, Mann über der Frau, „weiße“ Hautfarbe über alle anderen people of colour und Reiche über den Armen. (…)


Im Gegensatz zu früheren Phasen des Aufstiegs der extremen Rechten in Lateinamerika, die jeweils 30 Jahre andauerten, stützen sich die aktuellen Kräfte jedoch auf ein unvollständiges und kurzsichtiges Gesellschaftsprojekt, das wirtschaftlich gesehen den weltweiten Trends zuwiderläuft. (…)Doch wenn diese extreme Rechte kein hoffnungsvolles Wirtschaftsprogramm vorlegen kann, wieso verfügt sie dann trotzdem über eine beträchtliche Wählerschaft? Eine Ursache ist sicherlich die Enttäuschung über die progressiven Kräfte, die die Wirtschaftskrise (Inflation, Versorgungsengpässe, Rezession) nicht überwinden konnten. Doch diese Erklärung allein reicht nicht aus.


Die radikale Rechte zieht mit zwei Schwertern ins Feld, die ihre hohen Zustimmungswerte erklären: Zum einen ist es das Versprechen, einige der wichtigsten Gründe der Wirtschaftskrise zu bekämpfen, und zum anderen das Versprechen, den von der Krise Geschädigten moralische Wiedergutmachung widerfahren zu lassen. Das erste Schwert zerfällt rasch und unwiderruflich; das zweite jedoch wird mit feuriger Geschicklichkeit geschwungen. Der rachsüchtige Hass der neuen Staatsräson gegen Menschenrechte, Migrant:innen, Linke, Kommunist:innen, die Kirchnerist:innen, Indigene, Feministinnen oder jeden Anflug von sozialer Gleichheit spielt die Rolle einer kollektiven Buße, die vom gescheiterten Wohlstandsversprechen ablenkt. Wenn es schon keine glückliche Zukunft gibt, dann soll es wenigstens das Vergnügen an der Grausamkeit geben. Opfer sind diejenigen, die sich als unversöhnlich anders betrachten. Diese moralische Perversion der Hoffnung zerreißt das soziale Gefüge. Und auch wenn sie nur von kurzer Dauer ist, werden ihre Folgen für den gesellschaftlichen Zusammenhalt lange anhalten. Man kann ihr nicht allein mit umgekehrter Wut begegnen. Auch wenn in Krisenzeiten eine Personifizierung der Schuldigen für soziale Missstände notwendig ist – nur dass sie sich in diesem Fall auf eine winzige Minderheit der Mächtigen konzentriert –, ist vor allem eine mutige Wiederherstellung einer glaubwürdigen Hoffnung auf ein produktivistisches und auf soziale Gerechtigkeit ausgerichtetes Projekt erforderlich. Dieses Projekt muss in der Lage sein, die Fundamente der verkommenen wirtschaftlichen und mentalen Strukturen zu erschüttern. Denn damit die Linke wieder eine …

title: Salario giusto per chi?
content:
Il 24 giugno è diventato legge il decreto sul salario giusto. Accanto ad altre misure, il provvedimento interviene direttamente sul livello delle retribuzioni e, indirettamente, sul reddito e sulle modalità in cui si svolge la contrattazione; mettendo nelle mani dei capitalisti ulteriori strumenti per regolare a proprio vantaggio il mercato del lavoro.


Ancora una volta, ci troviamo di fronte ad un provvedimento che, accentuando il ruolo del governo nel controllo autoritario della società, attirando su questo stesso governo il malcontento di vasti strati della popolazione. Al tempo il provvedimento stesso svela la funzione effettiva del governo quale strumento della sete di profitto della borghesia, dimostrando con i fatti la validità della critica anarchica all’attuale modello di società, basata sul dominio politico ed economico da parte di una ristretta minoranza privilegiata.


La classe operaia e le classi sfruttate non hanno nulla da attendersi dalle loro istituzioni e dai loro rappresentanti: solo la loro organizzazione autonoma e unitaria, sulla base dell’autorganizzazione e dell’azione diretta, può contrastare il continuo peggioramento delle condizioni di vita e di lavoro e al tempo stesso creare le premesse per una nuova organizzazione della società, che superi il regime della proprietà privata e abbatta ogni forma di governo.


Il governo, con il decreto prima e con la sua trasformazione in legge poi, stravolge peraltro la gerarchia delle fonti su cui si basa il diritto del lavoro. Questa gerarchia vede al primo posto la Costituzione, poi le leggi ordinarie e poi la contrattazione; da notare che quest’ultima non può stravolgere quanto ordinato dalla Costituzione e dalle leggi ordinarie. Il testo approvato dal parlamento prevede invece una sorta di primato della contrattazione fra le parti: scompare ogni riferimento alla vita libera e dignitosa che dovrebbe essere assicurata dalla retribuzione corrisposta a chi fornisce la propria capacità lavorativa, secondo quanto previsto espressamente dalla Costituzione. Questa disposizione viene invece sostituita dal

riferimento al

 trattamento economico complessivo definito dai CCNL stipulati dalle organizzazioni dei datori di lavoro e dei lavoratori comparativamente più rappresentative sul piano nazionale.


Il rapporto di subordinazione che lega chi svolge lavoro dipendente al datore di lavoro, elemento che giustificava l’intervento dello Stato nel rapporto di lavoro – intervento comunque sempre volto a mantenere questa subordinazione – viene mascherato nel rapporto contrattuale, che diviene la base del trattamento economico di chi vende la propria capacità lavorativa.


È un ritorno ad una prassi liberale, già superata a parole dal corporativismo fascista, superamento poi recepito dalla Costituzione repubblicana e divenuto prassi comune in seguito alle lotte dell’autunno caldo.


Il completo abbandono dei salari operai alla discrezione dei capitalisti è ribadito dalle scelte dei sindacati confederali. Con l’ultima proposta per un accordo quadro sulle relazioni interconfederali CGIL, CISL e UIL si sono completamente subordinati di fronte alle richieste padronali e del governo. L’accettazione dell’indice IPCA NEI come riferimento per l’aumento delle retribuzioni nominali si traduce nella rinuncia alla difesa del potere d’acquisto, e quindi delle condizioni di vita per milioni di lavoratori e per le loro famiglie. Ma figuriamoci se questi sindacati pensano ad una redistribuzione del reddito a favore dei ceti sociali più svantaggiati e a danno dei profitti!


Il l

egame tra burocrazia sindacale e apparato statale è inevitabile: la principale fonte di entrate non sono le contribuzioni degli iscritti inseriti in attività produttive, sono i contributi dei pensionati e i compensi per i servizi di patronato. I sindacati maggiormente rappresentativi, poi, sono eredi diretti dei sindacati fascisti, e da questi hanno ereditato la subordinazione alla politica, giustificata in forme diverse ma concomitanti dalle burocrazie sindacali di ispirazione socialcomunista, cattolica o repubblicana.


Il processo di costruzione di un regime fascista, in atto oggi in Italia, non può che beneficiare dell’acquiescenza di CGIL, CISL e UIL.


Il benessere delle classi sfruttate, il loro elevamento materiale e morale, la loro emancipazione sta nelle loro mani, nella loro capacità di unirsi e dar vita ad organizzazioni stabili sotto il loro diretto controllo, autonome dai partiti e dalle …

author: Unknown
title: Acqua e Terre
content:
Perché un’azienda italiana del comparto digitale sta comprando centrali idroelettriche e miniere?


Da Orizzonti

*


Un’impresa privata italiana acquista centrali idroelettriche e miniere. Non siamo nel 1926, ma nel 2026, l’impresa in questione non produce tessuti, ma offre servizi internet.


E’ di pochi mesi fa infatti la notizia che Aruba ha comprato tre centrali idroelettriche in Piemonte

1

 e ha conquistato le quote di maggioranza della Società Mineraria Gerrei a Silius in Sardegna

2

. Perché un’azienda impegnata nel digitale fa investimenti in settori che richiamano l’alba del capitalismo industriale nel nostro paese?


Partiamo dall’inizio: Aruba è una società italiana fondata nel 1994 a Firenze, inizialmente forniva connessioni dial-up (per capirci la famosa 56k, quella col modem analogico che faceva i rumori e occupava la linea fissa telefonica di casa), poi offerte di registrazione di dominio per i siti internet ed hosting. Aruba apre un primo Data Center in Italia nel 2003 ad Arezzo a cui poi se ne affiancherà un secondo. Un terzo è stato costruito a Ponte San Pietro (Bergamo) nel 2017 all’interno di un ex-cotonificio ed è alimentato anche con energia idroelettrica. Infine un ultimo Data Center sul territorio italiano di livello hyperscaler

3

 è stato inaugurato nel 2024 a Roma all’interno del Tecnopolo Tiburtino

4

. Nel tempo l’azienda ha vantato collaborazioni con università, Pubblica Amministrazione e si è espansa a livello internazionale fornendo servizi in Europa Orientale e Centrale attraverso altri data center presenti in Germania, Francia, Inghilterra e Polonia. Nel panorama del capitalismo italiano Aruba è un’anomalia perché è riuscita a competere nel suo settore sul mercato europeo con i pesi massimi delle big tech statunitensi, pur rimanendo, nel solco delle dinastie della borghesia italiana, un’azienda a gestione familiare. Stefano Cecconi, amministratore delegato di Aruba, in una delle rare interviste

5

 reperibili in rete sintetizza così l’approccio:

“Siamo una società della new economy che ha avuto un approccio old economy. Non abbiamo cercato investitori esterni, ma semmai di reinvestire nella società. Non dobbiamo convincere della bontà di un progetto qualcun altro che non vive tutti i giorni il nostro settore. Il segreto di un’impresa familiare è la libertà di poter rischiare, la determinazione che si genera quando si lavora in proprio a tutti gli effetti e si rischia il patrimonio della famiglia stessa”

. Questa peculiarità oggi potrebbe rappresentare un vantaggio inaspettato, in tempi in cui la questione della sovranità nel campo dei dati e del digitale diventa un tema strategico sul piano geopolitico.


Ciò che rende il caso Aruba interessante per noi è proprio questa compresenza di elementi di estrema modernità integrati con il recupero di centralità di tecnologie, forme di organizzazione e modi di produzione che sembravano anticaglie del passato industriale italiano. Non c’è da stupirsi particolarmente, la rivoluzione dell’Intelligenza Artificiale richiede intensività ed estensività dello sfruttamento di risorse e lavoro. Questo significa che, come già successo in passato in occasione delle altre Rivoluzioni Industriali, la catena del valore torna a distendersi oltre che nello spazio, anche nel tempo recuperando in chiave nuova le tecnologie basali del capitalismo. Come scrivevamo

qui

:


Ogni grammo di materia prima, ogni goccia di sudore devono essere catturati per non rimanere indietro nella competizione globale.


Acqua


L’alba del capitalismo italiano si è basata quasi interamente sulla forza dell’acqua. Prima come fonte di energia diretta attraverso i mulini ad acqua che venivano utilizzati non solo per macinare i cereali, ma per azionare i mantici dei forni fusori, per attivare le pile idrauliche delle cartiere, per muovere le bielle delle segherie ecc… poi con l’idroelettrico. La disponibilità di acqua e legname resero le valli alpine tra i primi luoghi di insediamento industriale. Alcune di queste industrie insistevano su tradizioni precedenti, precapitalistiche, come il tessile nel biellese o l’industria armiera in Val Trompia.


Mappa dell’industrializzazione alpina nel periodo 1850-1880. Di Marcello Modica da

Revue de géographie alpine


La trasformazione dei paesaggi alpini fu impressionante e repentina. In molte delle valli interessate da questi primi cicli di industrializzazione esistono tutt’ora archeologie industriali di quell’epoca …

content:
Συνέντευξη με τον Αρτάν, μέλος της Αναρχικής Συλλογικότητας

Smokva

 των Σκοπίων, που διοργάνωσε το προ ημερών 18

ο

 Βαλκανικό Αναρχικό Φεστιβάλ Βιβλίου. Διατυπώνει μια πρώτη αποτίμηση, που επικεντρώθηκαν οι συζητήσεις, σε τι συνεισέφερε στα ευρύτερα ζητήματα και κυρίως ποιες αποφασίστηκε να είναι οι άμεσες δράσεις.


>Πώς αποτιμάται το 4ήμερο Βαλκανικό Αναρχικό Φεστιβάλ Βιβλίου στα Σκόπια;


Όπως είχαμε την ευκαιρία να συζητήσουμε, είχαμε μια πολύ ιδιαίτερη εμπειρία αυτού του φεστιβάλ στα Σκόπια. Αποτελεί μια από τις σημαντικές συνεισφορές στην περιοχή.


Τρία ή τέσσερα χρόνια πριν δεν θα είχαμε τέτοια δυνατότητα. Αλλά επειδή στο προηγούμενο ΒΑΒ στη Θεσσαλονίκη που ήμασταν περίπου 20 ακτιβιστές από εδώ γεννήθηκε η ιδέα να διεξαχθεί στα Σκόπια, κάτι που αποτέλεσε κίνητρο για εμάς και αμέσως αρχίσαμε την προετοιμασία του.


Έτσι άρχισε να ενεργοποιείται ένας κόσμος, ιδιαίτερα νεολαίοι που πριν δεν είχαν κάποια εμπλοκή με τα κινήματα. Κάτι που το είδαμε όλοι μας αυτές τις ημέρες με τη συμμετοχή τόσων ανθρώπων από την πόλη, εδώ.


>Σε ποια θέματα επικεντρώθηκαν οι εκδηλώσεις και συζητήσεις;


Ξεκινήσαμε από τοπικά ζητήματα της περιοχής αλλά και ευρύτερα διεθνή ζητήματα, όπως η γενοκτονία στη Γάζα και η διεθνιστική αλληλεγγύη στην Παλαιστίνη, η αντίδραση στον νέο μιλιταρισμό ιδιαίτερα στην Ευρώπη, η καταπίεση και καταστολή κα. Έτσι είχαμε αρκετές συζητήσεις πάνω σε αυτά τα θέματα και πώς θα οργανώσουμε την αντίστασή μας.


Επίσης, είχαμε συζητήσεις για τις πολιτικές, τους τρόπους οργάνωσης και τις κινητοποιήσεις ενάντια στον φασισμό στα Βαλκάνια, αλλά και στην Ευρώπη, και θα συνεχιστεί η συζήτηση μέχρι το επόμενο ΒΑΒ. Κάτι που αποτέλεσε συνεισφορά των συντρόφων που ήρθαν από ευρωπαϊκές χώρες, να μην περιοριστούμε στα Βαλκάνια αλλά ευρύτερα διεθνώς.


Άλλωστε τα Βαλκάνια σήμερα αποτελούν σημαντικό σημείο επικέντρωσης των αναρχικών διεθνώς. Και αυτό είναι ένα στοίχημα το πως μια βαλκανική οργάνωση μπορεί να συνεισφέρει ευρύτερα, κάτι που αναγνωρίζεται. Ήταν πρόκληση 14 χρόνια μετά την προηγούμενη διοργάνωση εδώ στα Σκόπια.


>Ποια μπορούμε να πούμε ότι είναι το σημαντικότερο χαρακτηριστικό αυτού του ΒΑΒ;


Νομίζω ένα από τα σημαντικότερα ήταν η μεγάλη συμμετοχή στις συνελεύσεις πάνω σε ζητήματα δράσης. Δεν μείναμε μόνο στο επίπεδο της κατάθεσης πολιτικών ιδεών αλλά στην επεξεργασία συγκεκριμένων βημάτων δράσης και όχι μόνο στα Βαλκάνια. Έτσι ελήφθησαν 3 συγκεκριμένες αποφάσεις.


Μια περιφερειακή και διεθνής αντιμιλιταριστική οργάνωση και μία ημέρα διεθνούς δράσης κατά του μιλιταρισμού. Όπως επίσης συζητήσαμε και για τον τόπο διοργάνωσης του επόμενου ΒΑΒ που θα καταληχθεί στον επόμενο μήνα.

author: Redazione_web
title: Sacco e Vanzetti. Assassinio di stato e solidarietà internazionale
content:
“Se l’anarchismo era la punta più avanzata di questa lotta per la libertà contro la tirannia, la documentazione più concreta di una battaglia-simbolo combattuta proprio dagli anarchici, quella sul caso Sacco e Vanzetti, rappresentava simbolicamente uno dei riferimenti più avanzati di questa forma di pensiero, che pertanto avrebbe potuto essere colpita in maniera tanto pesante quanto letale” – L.Botta Le carte di Vanzetti Aragno ed. Torino 2019 pag 42.


E ancora:


 “La salute è in voi” – lettera di Bartolomeo Vanzetti ai compagni nel 1927 – a cura di Robert D’Attilio ed. Il Picconiere – El Paso – Villafalletto Cuneo 2007.


Centosette anni fa, il 24 dicembre 1919 a Bridgewater nel Massachusetts, alcuni individui tentarono una rapina ad un blindato. Vanzetti fu accusato di questo. Era un militante anarchico conosciuto alla polizia, si era occupato di scioperi, aveva volantinato, diffondeva pubblicamente idee sovversive, scriveva ed era stimato tra la sua gente, immigrati italiani che quel giorno erano da lui al porto di Plymouth a comprare pesce secondo una atavica tradizione natalizia. Quando insieme con Sacco fu anche accusato della rapina a South Braintree del il 15 aprile 1920, era già ritenuto colpevole della tentata rapina di dicembre, non per sentenza di tribunale, ma perché anarchico, immigrato e renitente alla leva. Tutti reati, questi ultimi, che gli verranno rinfacciati nei 7 anni di tortura processuale iniziati dall’arresto, il 5 maggio 1920. Dei reati attribuitigli, nella requisitoria dell’aprile 1927, a sentenza definitiva, rivendicava la verità e la logica: “Se io potessi rinascere due volte, per due volte rifarei quello che ho fatto finora. Voi mi condannate perché sono italiano, ed in effetti io sono italiano, e voi mi condannate perché sono anarchico, e io sono anarchico”. Lo disse in piemontese “Mi sun anarchic!” e qualcuno tradusse.


Quindi, una volta conosciuta la cronaca del caso Sacco e Vanzetti e la loro innocenza sui reati specifici, si smetta di rimarcare il vittimismo di due anime innocenti, si smetta di fare feticismo degli eroi e si parli del perché della loro condanna: essi erano colpevoli di anarchismo e le loro idee erano incompatibili con la Red Scare americana. Ed erano colpevoli di essere stranieri. In effetti il caso Sacco e Vanzetti attraversa tutti i temi che sono comuni alla emigrazione. Temi tuttora attuali. Il motivo per cui si abbandona il proprio paese, il  cammino, l’attraversamento, l’arrivo al porto, la selezione ai confini, il respingimento o la detenzione provvisoria in attesa di essere o meno accolto, il mercato del lavoro, la ricerca della casa, che era abbinata al lavoro – se lo perdevi perdevi anche la casa. E poi le lotte per un contratto, il riconoscimento dei diritti civili, il movimento operaio dell’emigrazione, soprattutto della Costa Atlantica, nel quale era presente il movimento anarchico, l’anarchismo di Luigi Galleani, al quale Nick e Bart aderirono fin dal 1912, prima con contributi al giornale di Galleani “Cronaca Sovversiva”, poi con articoli, ma soprattutto con opera di agitazione, propaganda e partecipazione agli scioperi e alla controinformazione. Ricordiamo che quel sabato 5 maggio del 1920, quando furono arrestati, avevano volantini che informavano dell’assassinio di Andrea Salsedo da parte della BOI, che poi diventerà FBI, con la stessa modalità della morte di Pinelli. Nel 1917, i nostri erano stati insieme nel Messico, renitenti alla leva della prima guerra mondiale. Ed ancora il Caso Sacco e Vanzetti riguarda la giustizia di stato, la repressione, il circuito carcerario, la pena di morte. E durante il processo tutta la xenofobia dei funzionari bianchi – polizia e magistratura – verso gli emigrati, negando credibilità ai testimoni italiani, creando o nascondendo materiali processuali, e indirizzando i testimoni d’accusa.


Solo 50 anni dopo il governatore del Massachusetts, Michael Dukakis, figlio di emigrati, dichiarò a nome dello stato che quel processo era inficiato da razzismo e che ogni onta andava cancellata dalla memoria di Sacco e Vanzetti. Ricorda quella scena del film di Roberto Benigni in cui Johny Stecchino si chiede perché il boss Cozzamara ce l’avesse con lui: “Vabbeh, gli ho ammazzato la moglie, ma poi gli ho chiesto scusa. E che sarà mai!”.


Ne parlammo a Villafalletto, paese natale di Bart, nel sessantesimo dei fatti, nel settembre 1987, con la F.A.I., il Centro Studi Pinelli, lo storico Luigi Botta e l’Istituto Storico della …

For far too long, anarchism has been neglected, treated as a utopian dream that seems all but impossible to achieve, not just by those with little to no understanding of what anarchism is – but even by the anarchists themselves.

We anarchists are a disjointed and hard-to-define group, just as it should be. The anarchist believes that all people have the right to forge their own best life in a society based on voluntary association, equality and freedom, under the prerequisite that no one restricts or harms anyone else. We can all agree on that. For what is it that all anarchists want? To abolish the state and capitalism. The state that reduces us to expandable parts of a monstrous machinery and capitalism to serfs in an inhumane economy. We demand autonomous self-government for ourselves; to break free from the invalid social contract.

In my lifetime, I want to start changing that. I want to hand a better world to my children and their children; a life in greater freedom than to be wage slaves under illicit state control. That is the reality that all of us who call ourselves anarchists want to achieve, no matter what adjectives we use. The time has come to yet again speak about anarchism. To inform and to raise public awareness about what we believe in. It’s time to take anarchism seriously again. The road to the realisation of anarchy is long and arduous, but as with all truly positive change and progress, so too can this new reality take shape, slowly and small-scale at first, in order to then encompass a whole world.

To shout obscenities at the police and to encourage the killing of politicians is as effective as trying to light a fire with waterlogged wood without matches. We anarchists are those who stand to lose from such childishness. Put aside the romanticism of violent revolution and the belief that terror can create long-term change and improvement for people. All true anarchists want to create the best possible life for everyone. It is the polar opposite of nihilism – it is humanism. The road forward is to educate, enlighten and the use of direct action based on nonviolence. All violent means of action are not only counterproductive but also entirely irreconcilable with the right of all people to self-determination and freedom from the oppression of others, the foundations on which anarchism rests. Otherwise, we are no better than the fascists or communists. True freedom and equality is not achieved by ruining someone else’s life, but by defending everyone’s life.

And in a genuine anarchist society, all voices get to be heard: an individualist anarchist and an anarcho-communist should have equal opportunity to shape their lives the way they find most suitable. Theoretical discussions are always welcome, but the most important thing is to create the conditions for anarchy – the abolishment of the state and of capitalism. That which comes after, that comes after. For a long time, other causes and movements (all highly honourable of course) have taken up a lot of time for many …

author: radical.guide
title: The Revolt of Care: Anarchist Mutual Aid in 21st Century
content:
The death of God did not free us from domination. It tore the social fabric, emboldened the profiteers, and left us alone in front of a silent, cold, and indifferent universe: the capitalist universe. Traditional communities were dissolved, and what replaced them was not the insurgent commune but the depression of the isolated nuclear family and the loneliness of the careerist. Our societies have not rejected the need for tenderness and care.


They have covered it with a hard irony that makes it look unnecessary, naive, obsolete. Anxiety, precarity, debt and exhaustion are handed back to us as individual failures, and the loneliness that follows is not an accident of the system but one of its products. This talk proposes that care, when it is born not as charity or duty, but as shared resistance to oppression, is a revolutionary act.


Drawing on Kropotkin's ethics of mutual aid, on Anselm Jappe and Christopher Lasch on narcissism as the psychic form of late capitalism, and on The Care Collective, bell hooks and Judith Butler, it traces how diffuse fear is converted into hatred of the weak, the foreigner and the different, and how that individualism, neo-conformism, indifference and social apathy are the engines of contemporary fascism. Freedom that ends where the needs of another begin is not freedom. It is privilege. Against this, the talk proposes Anarchist Politics of the Living: open coexistence, full symbiotic inclusion, reciprocity, radical interdependence, equality of all living beings, and an attack against all authorities of this world. The working class today includes everyone losing the right to exist, to breathe, to move, to protest: the poor stripped of healthcare, trans people stripped of legal rights, migrants held in camps, rescuers of shipwrecked refugees prosecuted as criminals, students arrested inside their universities for opposing genocide. After thirty and forty years of separated single-issue struggles, feminism, queer life, anarcho-communism, labour, autonomy, radical ecology, counterculture, a generation is now looking for the points where these struggles converge. Care is one of them. Care does not aim to fix. It aims to accompany. It is the embodied reminder that nothing human is small or unworthy. The talk is based on the essay "The Revolt of Care", written by Tasos Sagris as a member of the revolutionary symbiotic community Void Network and growing directly out of the collective's long-running discussions on mutual aid and collective love. Void Network has organized political and cultural counter-institutions, festivals, occupations and free public gatherings in Athens since 1990.


The essay is not the position of an author or a theoretician but an attempt to formulate what a community has been working through together, and it comes to the fair in that spirit: unfinished, open to challenge, and meant to be continued in open assemblies.


THE OPEN DISCUSSION


The second half is a collective, non-hierarchical conversation. Proposed openings: How do we build structures of free care that do not reproduce hierarchy, professionalism or charity? How do we care for those who carry the work of caring, in occupations, squats, collectives and communities of struggle? How do we practice care as antifascist infrastructure rather than as private virtue? What do we do with our own hardness? Participants are invited to bring concrete experiences from their own projects. The aim is not conclusions but a shared inventory of practices.


BIO:


Tasos Sagris is an anarchist poet, theater director and political essayist, born in Athens in 1972. In 1990 he co-founded the international anarchist collective Void Network. He is co-editor, with A.G. Schwarz and Void Network, of We Are an Image from the Future: The Greek Revolt of December 2008 (AK Press, 2010), which he presented on a book tour across thirty US states. His poetry books include About Human Love in the Western Metropolitan Cities (2008), Phenomenology of the Guillotine (2018), The Ocean of Chronos (2026). He has directed theater shows (The Maids by Jean Genet, Metamorphosis by Franz Kafka, 4.48 Psychosis by Sarah Kane) and festivals in occupied and public spaces. For the last 15 years, he has participated in the open assembly of the occupied Free Self-Organised Theater Embros in Athens. He tours regularly in Europe, Asia, Mexico, and the USA for talks and spoken-word performances. He has participated in social movements in Greece and …

author: Unknown
title: La bombe n'est pas à nous : pourquoi les anarchistes reparlent de l'arme nucléaire
content:
Lyon, le 22 septembre. Alors que les États augmentent leurs budgets militaires et modernisent leurs arsenaux nucléaires, les services sociaux ferment et les militant·es sont poursuivi·es. Les groupes anarchistes et antimilitaristes lyonnais appellent à relier la lutte contre l'arme nucléaire aux conflits sociaux du quotidien — et à descendre dans la rue pour une marche contre l'arme nucléaire à la fin du mois.


Ce qui se passe


Les dépenses mondiales consacrées aux programmes nucléaires continuent d'augmenter, malgré les déclarations sur le désarmement. La France, qui fait partie des puissances nucléaires, conserve et modernise son arsenal — tout en réduisant le financement des hôpitaux, des écoles et du logement social. Les sites militaires restent des zones de secret et de répression : les manifestations y sont interdites, les militant·es poursuivi·es, l'information verrouillée.


Pourquoi ça nous concerne


Pour les anarchistes, l'arme nucléaire n'est pas une menace abstraite : c'est la forme ultime du pouvoir étatique. La décision de vie ou de mort de millions de personnes est prise par une poignée d'individus, tandis que les conséquences pèsent sur tout le monde. Chaque euro investi dans des ogives est un euro volé aux hôpitaux, aux écoles et au logement. La logique qui sous-tend l'arsenal nucléaire est la même que celle qui sous-tend le déblocage des camps, l'expulsion des squats et l'interdiction des grèves.


Nous ne pouvons pas «

 

faire sauter

 

» les arsenaux seuls. Mais nous pouvons dénoncer le militarisme, relier la lutte pour le logement et le climat à la critique de la machine de guerre, soutenir les initiatives antinucléaires — et construire des structures horizontales plutôt que des verticales de la peur.


Ce que nous pouvons faire


Venir aux actions antinucléaires et antiguerre — marches, piquets, blocages.


Soutenir les grèves et les mouvements sociaux — relier le militarisme à l'exploitation quotidienne.


Exiger la transparence des budgets militaires et dénoncer la propagande de la «

 

sécurité

 

».


Construire l'entraide et des réseaux de solidarité locaux.


📢 Marche contre l'arme nucléaire — Lyon


Samedi 17 octobre, 14h00


Rassemblement : Place Bellecour, Lyon


Itinéraire : Bellecour → Préfecture → Base aérienne 942 (Mont Verdun)


Nous ne descendons pas seulement contre la bombe. Nous descendons contre l'État qui dépense pour la guerre ce qui nous est volé. Contre le militarisme qui tue ici et maintenant — à Gaza, en Ukraine, au Soudan et dans nos rues. Contre le pouvoir qui décide à notre place si nous vivons ou non.


Revendications de la marche :


Réduction des dépenses militaires et réorientation des moyens vers les services sociaux.


Fermeture des sites nucléaires et des bases militaires sur le territoire.


Liberté de manifester et fin des poursuites contre les antimilitaristes.


Non à la guerre — ici comme partout.


Apportez : banderoles, pancartes, instruments de musique, de l'eau, de la solidarité. Bloc de solidarité avec les grèves sociales — rassemblement à 13h30 à Place Guichard (près de la sortie du métro, Lyon 3

e

).


Toutes les annonces, la logistique et le contact — sur Telegram : t.me/Stop_Bombe_Lyon


La bombe n'est pas à nous. Elle appartient au pouvoir qui ne nous a pas consulté·es. Venez — et montrez que la décision doit être la nôtre, pas la leur.


Note sur le lieu : la Base aérienne 942 (Mont Verdun) est un site militaire réel de la région lyonnaise, situé au nord de Lyon (Monts d'Or). Elle abrite un centre de commandement souterrain et joue un rôle dans la défense aérienne et la dissuasion. Elle a déjà été la cible d'actions directes de militant·es antinucléaires dans les années 1970, ce qui rend ce point d'arrivée symboliquement et historiquement cohérent.

author: Joshua W.J. Brown
title: The New Native Needs a Theory of Obligation, Not a Blood Test
content:
The New Native should not become the old Native with a better genealogy.


That is the danger I keep hearing underneath the question

The Elephant

 has been asking this year. The “New Native” in this series is not a newly discovered ethnic group. It is a political figure emerging from a Kenyan public that has begun to act as though citizenship might mean more than being represented upward by an ethnic kingpin, disciplined by a church, managed by a civil servant, or frightened back into the inherited categories of the colonial state.


Akal Mohan sees the consolidation of a Kenyan identity beyond old orders of tribe, clan and denomination. Wangui Kimari traces the state’s fear of the “detribalized native”, then and now: the urban African who does not stay where authority says identity belongs. Joe Kobuthi reads the 2024 rupture through theology and the failure of a state that has demanded something close to sacred obedience. Across the series, the New Native becomes legible precisely when older intermediaries stop being able to explain the citizen to himself.


But once “native” is liberated from colonial administration, a second problem arrives. What is it going to mean?


If native means only ancestry, the term can become a blood test. If it means only citizenship, it can become historical amnesia. Neither answer is adequate for a country in which people can be equal citizens while communities still possess radically unequal historical relationships to land, dispossession, state violence, migration and political power.


Kenya’s own constitution already knows this, even when political language forgets.


One country, more than one kind of right


Chapter Three of the constitution does not grade citizenship by antiquity. A Kenyan citizen is a citizen. Citizenship may be acquired by birth or registration, and citizens possess the rights, privileges and benefits of that status. The constitution does not say that a person becomes more Kenyan because his ancestors arrived first, or less Kenyan because a grandparent crossed a border.


Then Chapter Five does something equally important: it refuses to pretend that equal citizenship has dissolved collective history. Article 63 recognizes community land, including ancestral lands and lands traditionally occupied by hunter-gatherer communities. The Community Land Act recognizes customary rights and gives them legal force. Article 56 requires affirmative measures for minorities and marginalized groups.


These provisions are not an embarrassing inconsistency in the constitutional order. They are a clue.


Equal citizenship and historically specific rights can coexist because they answer different questions. Citizenship asks: who belongs to the political community, and on what civic terms? Ancestral land rights ask: what relationship does a particular community possess to a particular place, and what happened to that relationship? A remedy for dispossession is not a superior passport. A passport is not a land restitution programme.


Conflate those categories and the state gets two convenient escapes. It can tell a dispossessed community that everyone is equal now, therefore the old theft no longer requires a specific remedy. Or it can tell citizens descended from later-arriving populations that they may live under the law but can never fully belong because history placed their ancestors in the wrong column.


Both moves turn time into an alibi.


The Ogiek case is about more than recognition


The Ogiek litigation makes the first danger impossible to romanticize away.


In 2017, the African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights found Kenya responsible for violations involving Ogiek land, property, natural resources, culture and development. In 2022, the Court ordered reparations, including compensation and measures to secure Ogiek ancestral land rights. In December 2025, after years of implementation failure, the Court found Kenya had still not made the ordered compensation payments, had not completed the identification, delimitation, demarcation and collective titling of Ogiek ancestral land, and had not begun the consultations required to resolve concessions and leases affecting that land.


That matters to the New Native argument because it shows why a purely civic vocabulary is insufficient. “We are all Kenyans” cannot do the work of a title, a payment, a boundary, a consultation, or the restoration of a legal relationship to ancestral land.


Universal equality is not the …

author: Nada Elia
title: Women and Youth Are at the Forefront of the Struggle for Palestinian Liberation
content:
They follow in the footsteps of Palestinian women and children who have resisted colonialism in the past century.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

I grew up in a household of women and children that, as my sisters and I matured, eventually became a household of only women. My father was frequently gone on long overseas business trips before his untimely death when I was seven. I often wonder if this is the reason the expression “women and children” strikes me as essentially flawed: It suggests that women and children are the more vulnerable members of society, rather than its resilient survivors. It infantilizes women by grouping them with children, rather than adult men.

In the context of a national struggle, it strips women of agency, as if such agency can only manifest through armed revolt. In a military context, the expression “women and children” — or “womenandchildren,” to use the term coined by antimilitary feminist scholar Cynthia Enloe — presumes that women and children never take up arms or participate in resistance, even as we see such actions occurring in numerous struggles around the world. And in listing casualties, it implies that men’s deaths and injuries are less tragic, less mournable.

In the case of Palestine, women and youth have led, and continue to lead, some of the most transformative efforts and initiatives in our people’s quest for justice — that is, our resistance first to imperialism, then to settler colonialism and apartheid. They have not been spared Israel’s violence, just for being women, or children, and many have been and remain at the forefront of popular resistance to Zionism’s ultimate aim of eliminating all Palestinians. While this may have become more obvious during Israel’s accelerated genocidal assault on Gaza following Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attacks, it had always been clear to anyone not deliberately looking away.

From a number of uprisings over the past century in Palestine, it is obvious that youth, “the children,” are not just among the leaders; they are the more effective, more transformational leaders. Unfettered by traditions and social norms they do not relate to, they engage in novel forms of organizing, seeking the complete abolition of oppressive systems, rather than their reversal. And women, in their capacity as autonomous adults, rather than merely as wives and mothers, have consistently resisted both the imperial ideology targeting their country, and the military assaults that accompanied it. They did so while providing men, as well as the youth and children, the moral, emotional, and practical support the Palestinian people need in order to persist. This was perhaps most evident on a global scale during the 1987–93 Intifada, when women organized most of the popular committees tending to the educational, nutritional, and health needs of Palestinians resisting Israel’s clampdown, as youth took to the streets daily to express their rejection of Israel’s decades-long oppressive rule. These defenseless children hurled rocks at armored tanks, fully aware of the hefty price they would pay for their defiant act, because they knew that risking limb and life is preferable to living without freedom and dignity.

Women’s and children’s agency is enacted daily in the courage of girls such as Janna Jihad, who was dubbed “the world’s youngest journalist” when she started documenting Israel’s crimes at a mere seven years of age. Jihad started recording Israel’s attacks using her mother’s cell phone, posting her recordings far and wide on social media. She has repeatedly said that her camera is her weapon of choice. Jihad is the cousin of Ahed Tamimi, the “lioness” who has confronted heavily armed Israeli soldiers determined to take over her village lands since she was a toddler. Israel imprisoned Tamimi for eight months when she was sixteen; she used the time behind bars to read up on international law, later enrolling in college planning to go to law school, so as to hold Israel accountable for its violations. “I am a freedom fighter. So I will not be the victim,” she told journalists upon her release.

Palestinian children’s agency was also clear in the 2022 uprising of rebellious youth standing up to Israel’s might. Ibrahim al-Nabulsi, dubbed “the Lion of Nablus,” was eighteen when he was brutally assassinated by the Israeli Occupation Forces. Following his martyrdom, his mother, Huda al-Nabulsi …

author: Yohannes Woldemariam
title: Imperial Nostalgia: History, Sovereignty, and the Unfinished Work of Decolonization in the Horn of Africa
content:
History in the Horn of Africa is rarely allowed to remain history. An ancient civilization becomes evidence of modern sovereignty. A medieval dynasty becomes proof of national continuity. Territory incorporated during one political era is later remembered as though it had always belonged to the state that governed it.


This habit has become especially visible as the Red Sea has returned to Ethiopian political discourse. Ethiopia is landlocked and has obvious economic reasons to seek dependable maritime trade. But there is a fundamental difference between negotiating the use of a port and claiming that a neighboring country possesses territory that properly belongs to Ethiopia. That distinction disappears when Assab is described as a “lost Ethiopian port.”


Ethiopia did not lose a sovereign port in 1993. Eritrea recovered sovereignty over territory that had been incorporated into Ethiopia after the violation and eventual termination of an internationally established federal arrangement. To describe this as Ethiopia “losing the sea” begins the story at the moment of Ethiopian possession and ignores how that possession came about.


This is what I mean by imperial nostalgia.


Imperial nostalgia is not merely admiration for emperors or attachment to an earlier age. It is a way of remembering political space. Territory once incorporated into an empire is remembered not simply as territory once governed, but as territory that naturally belonged there. Incorporation becomes ownership, ownership becomes entitlement, and independence can then be remembered as national loss.


Christopher Clapham’s notion of an Ethiopian “manifest destiny” is useful at the margins of this argument, although I invoke him cautiously and not to validate Ethiopian historical claims. The phrase captures a mentality in which expansion can stop looking like expansion when incorporation is presented as the fulfillment of history. Manifest destiny looks forward. Imperial nostalgia looks backward and imagines that a geography produced through expansion was the natural order all along.


The deeper problem is the projection of modern states backward into political worlds that did not organize themselves according to contemporary borders. Aksum is an obvious example. Its political and commercial world crossed territories that are now divided between Eritrea and Ethiopia and formed part of a much larger Red Sea system.

UNESCO’s account of Aksum

 describes an ancient civilization. It does not describe a modern territorial state possessing a contemporary claim to the Red Sea.


Calling Aksum simply “ancient Ethiopia” imports the political geography of today into antiquity. Calling it “ancient Eritrea” would make the same mistake. Civilizations, languages, religions, trading networks, and archaeological landscapes regularly cross the boundaries of modern states. Shared history does not create shared sovereignty.


I explored this problem more fully in

There Is No Timeless Eritrea or Ethiopia

. The point is not to diminish the history of either country. It is to stop asking ancient civilizations to perform the work of modern territorial law. Aksum should be studied as Aksum rather than recruited into a contemporary argument over Assab.


Richard Reid examined this problem directly in

The Trans-Mereb Experience: Perceptions of the Historical Relationship between Eritrea and Ethiopia

. Reid is useful because he is skeptical of efforts on either side to recruit antiquity into modern nationalism. The same history can be arranged to prove a supposedly eternal Ethiopia or, in the opposite direction, an Eritrea with no meaningful historical relationship to communities south of the Mereb. Neither approach is good history.


Even the word Ethiopia should make us cautious. The Greek term

Aithiopia

 did not refer neatly to the bounded territorial state called Ethiopia today. Recognizing this does not make modern Ethiopia less legitimate. It simply acknowledges that political names, communities, and territorial states change over time.


Eritrea should be approached in exactly the same way. Fred Halliday, writing in 1971 while the Eritrean war was still underway, acknowledged in

“The Fighting in Eritrea”

 that Eritrea in its modern territorial form had been defined under European colonialism. That fact does not weaken Eritrean sovereignty. It places Eritrea within the history of modern Africa.


Most African states inherited territorial forms created or …

Depuis 1853, les

kanak

 ont été relégués géographiquement, économiquement et politiquement dans leur propre pays. Ils ont été dépossédés de leurs terres, ce qui revient pour eux à la perte de leur identité. Ils ont vu aussi leurs moyens de subsistance s'amoindrir et leurs sites sacrés confisqués.


De 1888 à 1946, ils furent confinés dans des réserves et régis par le Code de l'indigénat qui les maintenait en dehors du droit commun.


Les Kanak ont toujours manifesté leur opposition à cette colonisation, mais les incessants soulèvements furent tous réprimés brutalement par l'administration française.


Parmi les plus mémorables résistances, il y a le soulèvement de 1878 conduits par Ataï et d'autres chefs kanak visant la prise de la capitale, Nouméa,

à la date anniversaire du 24 septembre

.


Le 24 septembre est devenu une date anniversaire, symbolisant la prise de possession du pays par la France, marquant le début de la colonisation. C'est une journée de deuil pour le peuple kanak.


A de nombreuses reprises, la date anniversaire a été symboliquement reprise :


Pierre Declercq

, leader indépendantiste de l'

 Le

Front de Libération Nationale Kanak et Socialiste

author: Paul Tiyambe Zeleza
title: The Historiographical Legacy of B.A. Ogot and His Generation
content:
Good evening, colleagues, and the Governor of Kisumu County, Professor Anyang Nyong’o! It is truly a pleasure for me to join you in this commemoration of the towering historian, scholar, and public intellectual, Bethwell Alan Ogot. I believe I speak on behalf of all of us in extending our deep gratitude to the Council for the Development of Social Science Research in Africa (CODESRIA) and the Department of History at Kenyatta University for organizing this important conference. Personally, my appreciation extends to that rarity of experiences, the opportunity to meet several of my former students at Kenyatta University between 1984 and 1989 who have become distinguished academics and administrators. It’s a befitting tribute to our intellectual father, grandfather, quickly becoming a great-grandfather, who was raised and spent his last years and is buried in nearby Yala, that this conference is being held in his home city of Kisumu, under the transformative leadership of one of Kenya’s leading scholars and public intellectuals, Governor Peter Anyang Nyong’o.


Introduction


Let me begin by noting that I last visited Kisumu in January 2019 to join Professor Ogot as he celebrated his 90th birthday. I first visited this city nearly forty years earlier, in 1980, when I was doing research for my doctoral dissertation on Kenyan economic and labor history, and spent time at this venue, the Tom Mboya Labor College. Professor Ogot had a lot to do with my interest in Kenyan history. My engagement with him goes back to 1976 when he served as external examiner at the University of Malawi.


Years later, he would proudly tell audiences at events where both of us were present that I owed my degree with distinction to him! In our classes on East African history, we had read Ogot’s books, and it was an indescribable honor and privilege to meet him in person. I was deeply touched and humbled when he asked to meet the student who had received the distinction, and he prevailed upon the department to bring me to the cottage along Lake Malawi, where the department took him to show their gratitude for bestowing the department with the distinction of his presence. .


That was the beginning of a lifelong mentoring and intellectual relationship that changed the trajectory of my personal and professional life, on which I will say more later.


When Professor Ogot passed away in January 2025, there was an avalanche of tributes in the popular and academic media celebrating his life and immense scholarly contributions. It is befitting that we are gathered here to remember and celebrate him as a towering historian and intellectual polymath.


Ogot belongs to an exceptional generation of the pioneering architects of the African academy in its multifaceted epistemic and institutional dimensions. These were extraordinary individuals, inspired by the fierce historical and humanistic urgency and imperatives of African nationalism: decolonization, nation-building, regional integration, development, and democracy. They were driven by the audacity, passion, and commitment to remaking the production, dissemination, and consumption of knowledge in, and for, Africa and the world.


They were scholar-activists who transformed existing disciplines and founded new ones, who built interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary paradigms, perspectives and practices, who believed in the power of education as a public good and engine of development, who relished their role as rigorous academics and public intellectuals, who jealously guarded academic freedom and the intelligentsia as the conscience of their new nation-states.


Their lives were large, complex, and multilayered. The trajectory of Ogot’s career is quite emblematic of his peers, born between the third and fourth decades of the twentieth century in the immediate aftermath of the formation of the colonial conquest state, whose ideologues deluded themselves would last for centuries, if not millennia, only to collapse spectacularly as Ogot and his peers matured into adulthood. I would like to explore, rather briefly given the limitations of time, five aspects of Professor Ogot’s remarkable life and legacy: Ogot the man, the historian, the institution builder, the public figure, and the mentor. Let me add that today we’ve heard much about many of these themes. My excuse for revisiting them is that I came a long way, and I have to justify my ticket!


Ogot the Man


Biographical reflections and commemorations …

content:
Samedi 26 septembre à 19h à la Kunda, à Vitry-sur-Seine, Survie organise une soirée contre le colonialisme chimique, en vue de la manifestation unitaire du 3 octobre contre les pesticides. Avec Syndicat des Travailleurs·ses Saisonnier·ères de la Filière Canne à Sucre (

STRASCAS

) du Cameroun, l'Observatoire Terre-Monde (

OTM

), le collectif Vietnam Dioxine et les Soulèvements de la Terre. Suivi d'un concert de Martial Pa'nucci.


Soirée contre le colonialisme chimique : nos corps et nos terres ne sont pas à vendre

 

!


Samedi 26 septembre à 19h à la Kunda, à Vitry-sur-Seine, Survie organise une soirée contre le colonialisme chimique, en vue de la manifestation unitaire du 3 octobre contre les pesticides.


Réunion publique sur la mobilisation contre les pesticides du 3 octobre


 |&nbsp30 août


Le samedi 5 septembre à 19h au Cirque Électrique, Place du Maquis du Vercors, 75020 aura lieu une soirée d'information sur la mobilisation contre pesticides prévue le 3 octobre près de l'usine Syngenta dans l'Eure


Le colonialisme chimique est presque absent des intérêts des luttes écologiques. Pourtant, il est bien au cœur du système impérial de domination. Dominer le vivant c'est aussi lui imposer des substances qui empoisonnent et détruisent. Mais le colonialisme chimique ne relève pas que de l'atteinte au Vivant. En realité, il ne vise pas tout le vivant. Précisément parce qu'il est colonial, le colonialisme chimique se repose sur une certitude : Celle que la valeur des corps, des êtres, du vivant et des lieux dits du «

 

Sud global

 

» n'ont pas la même valeur que celleux de l'Occident. La suprémacisme blanc s'accommode bien de cette incohérence. Il protège les forêts ici tout en participant massivement à la déforestation. Il interdit les pesticides ici tout en contaminant des populations entières ailleurs.


C'est pour mettre en lumière ce système et trouver des lieux de luttes communs que nous organisons cette soirée


avec des collectifs en lutte au Cameroun, aux Caraïbes, au Vietnam et en France, suivis d'un concert du rappeur anticolonial Martial Pa'nucci.


Les intervenant-es :


A. , du Syndicat des Travailleurs·ses Saisonnier·ères de la Filière Canne à Sucre (

STRASCAS

) du Cameroun, viendra témoigner des conditions de travail dans les plantations. Les travailleur·ses que représente le syndicat luttent contre des salaires très faibles, des protections sociales insuffisantes ainsi que leur exposition aux accidents du travail et aux pesticides sans équipements de protection adaptés. Ils et elles travaillent pour une filiale de la multinationale française Castel.


L'Observatoire Terre-Monde (

OTM

) est une association et plateforme de recherche en lutte pour imposer une écologie décoloniale. Ils participent à la lutte contre l'empoisonnement de masse au chlordecone.


Le collectif Vietnam Dioxine, lutte pour faire reconnaître les conséquences sanitaires et environnementales de l'Agent orange. Des décennies après son utilisation massive durant la guerre du Vietnam, les effets de la dioxine continuent de peser sur les populations.


Les Soulèvements de la Terre seront également présents pour parler des mobilisations actuelles contre l'industrie des pesticides et préparer la manifestation unitaire du 3 octobre.


La soirée se poursuivra avec un concert de Martial Pa'nucci, rappeur-activiste et poète urbain congolais, membre et cofondateur du mouvement citoyen

RAS

-

LE

-

BOL

author: Céli Pinto
title: The Most Important Election in Brazilian History
content:
We usually say that in general elections, we’re choosing a president, governors and lawmakers for the next four years. That much seems obvious. But in this election, with the first round on October 4 and the runoff on October 25, we’re not just choosing who governs. We’re choosing the country’s future for decades to come.

This isn’t a choice between candidate A and candidate B. It’s a choice between a sharp lurch toward colonized totalitarianism and the survival of democracy. Every voter needs to have this clearly in mind. We are responsible for this country’s future. Future generations will blame us, and rightly so, if we fail and Brazil is handed over to colonizer vultures.

Voters, whether or not they are politically active, whether they are young, middle-aged or elderly, have plenty of issues with the current government. It’s true the government could have done more, particularly if it didn’t have a Congress dedicated almost exclusively to serving its own interests. Even so, the government accomplished a great deal. It did this not despite Congress, but because Congress exists. That made it possible to negotiate with lawmakers and to pressure them through the press and social media.

We can only keep doing that if we also fight to change how Congress does politics. Everyone who wants to speak must be free to speak. Everyone must be free to fight politically. Institutions must be able to investigate, and to be investigated in turn. That means guaranteeing elections that are completely free and fair. None of this is possible unless we secure the survival of democracy, problems and all.

Voters, activists, young, middle-aged and elderly people all have good reason to be frustrated with the Supreme Court. There is a glaring indecency in the conduct of this group of mostly older men, all of them white. As for the court’s only woman, who is conservative, there hasn’t been a single incident involving her conduct as a public official.

But we live in a democracy. The only reason we weren’t overrun by the attempt to sabotage the 2022 election, and later by the attempt to pardon the military officers and their allies behind a heavily armed coup, is that the Superior Electoral Court and the Supreme Court exist. And the only reason we even know what’s happening now is that we live in a democracy, where everything can come to light.

The Trump administration is deepening its imperialist policy to alarming levels, even for those of us who have always understood the United States’ colonial ethos. This current phase of capitalism has abandoned even its weak pretense of democratic values. It now advances unbridled on the autonomy and sovereignty of countries in the Global South, especially in Latin America.

When President Lula said, in his address at the opening session of the U.N. General Assembly, that “Brazil doesn’t fit in anyone’s backyard,” he knew exactly what he was saying. Like many of us, he knows that a plot against Brazilian sovereignty is being assembled, led by the Bolsonaro family and its most obvious financial backers. Everyone involved would be pardoned if the worst were to happen, and the country would be driven into misery and excess.

This is a moment of absolute gravity. Circumstances like these have to be confronted directly, without half measures. If Lula wins the election, paradise won’t arrive overnight. Many people will keep facing frustrations. But I can assure you of this: no one will take the food out of people’s mouths, or the roof from over their heads, their universal right to public health through the Unified Public Health System (Brazil’s Sistema Único de Saúde, or SUS), or free medications, or the economic and racial quotas in education and public sector hiring.

If Lula wins, Brazil won’t magically become a country free of violence. Men won’t stop killing women in the senseless way they do today. But you can be certain that fewer poor, Black youth will die, and that police will be held accountable more often for mass killings.

The government will keep fighting organized crime, as it does now, by cutting off criminal factions’ money and arresting their leaders, including the politicians among them. There won’t be spectacular massacres like the one carried out by a police force whose state governor stands accused of colluding with the commanders responsible for the 122 deaths in October 2025 in Rio de Janeiro’s Complexo do Alemão favela.

Voting for Lula in this election isn’t voting for a …
